questions.question: An organization takes control of another company through acquisition and discovers the acquired company's security standards are significantly weaker, creating defense gaps. Which organizational change scenario is this, and what specifically mitigates the risk?
questions.option_a: Acquisitions; conduct a security assessment and review/adjust oncoming access controls
questions.option_b: Mergers; perform a security audit and use network segmentation tools
questions.option_c: Divestitures; use DLP tools and perform a security audit
questions.option_d: Staffing changes; properly manage account additions and departures
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Acquisitions involve one organization taking control of another, often requiring integration of systems/data/processes -- risks increase if the acquired company's security standards differ, creating defense gaps -- mitigated by conducting a security assessment and reviewing/adjusting oncoming access controls.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Mergers consolidate two companies into ONE new entity (a different structural change than one organization taking CONTROL of another), and its mitigation focuses on audits/segmentation/SIEM rather than specifically reviewing oncoming access controls.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Divestitures are the sale/separation of business assets (the opposite direction of an acquisition), mitigated by DLP and audits, not specifically the access-control review described for acquisitions.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Staffing changes involve individual employee additions/departures creating access control gaps -- a narrower, ongoing HR-driven risk, not the large-scale, whole-company security-standard mismatch risk of an acquisition.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 27: Attack Surface Determination
questions.explanation: Acquisitions (one org taking control of another) risk defense gaps when the acquired company's security standards differ -- mitigated by security assessment and reviewing/adjusting oncoming access controls, distinct from Mergers (consolidation risk, mitigated by audits/segmentation/SIEM) and Divestitures (data exposure risk, mitigated by DLP/audits).

questions.question: A security team is evaluating an already-deployed, currently operating production system -- identifying threats relevant to its existing architecture and operations and selecting appropriate mitigating controls. Which threat modeling approach is this, as opposed to one used for a system that doesn't yet exist?
questions.option_a: Modeling with an Existing IT System
questions.option_b: Modeling without an Existing IT System
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Modeling with an Existing IT System evaluates threats, vulnerabilities, exploits, and necessary security controls for a system already in operation -- identifying threats relevant to the system's current architecture/operations and selecting appropriate mitigating controls.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Modeling without an Existing IT System assesses threats/vulnerabilities for UNDEVELOPED systems, identifying risks before development/deployment -- the opposite of evaluating an already-operating production system.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Architecture Reviews are a Technical Attack Surface activity performed at the BEGINNING of a new system's design (using Threat Dragon) -- not specifically the evaluation of an already-deployed operating system's existing threats/controls.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. BC/DR Testing verifies disaster recovery strategies work -- an entirely different activity from threat modeling an existing system's architecture and operations.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 27: Attack Surface Determination
questions.explanation: Modeling with an Existing IT System evaluates threats/vulnerabilities/controls for a system already in place, identifying threats relevant to its current architecture/operations -- contrasted with Modeling without an Existing IT System, which assesses risk for undeveloped systems before deployment via four anticipatory steps.

questions.question: A SIEM tool links a failed login attempt on one server with an unusual outbound connection from a different server minutes later, recognizing these as parts of the same attack rather than isolated events. Which aggregate data analysis concept is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Correlation is the process of linking related events across different data sources -- SIEM tools can perform data correlation, recognizing that seemingly separate events (a failed login here, an unusual connection there) are actually part of the same coordinated activity.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Audit Log Reduction filters out irrelevant/low-priority logs to focus analysis -- a volume-reduction activity, not the linking-related-events-across-sources activity (Correlation) described.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Prioritization assigns importance to detected issues based on potential impact -- it happens AFTER events are identified/linked, not the linking activity itself.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Trends help spot recurring vulnerabilities or attack vectors over time by finding patterns in data -- a longer-term pattern-identification activity, not the immediate linking of two specific related events (Correlation).
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 28: Monitoring and Response
questions.explanation: Aggregate Data Analysis includes Audit Log Reduction (filtering low-priority logs), Correlation (linking related events across data sources, often via SIEM), Prioritization (ranking issues by impact), and Trends (spotting recurring patterns needing long-term mitigation) -- Correlation specifically connects seemingly separate events into a coherent attack picture.

questions.question: A security researcher reports a previously unknown vulnerability to a software vendor through a formal program that rewards them for responsible disclosure. Which threat intelligence source category is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Bounty Programs encourage security researchers to identify and report vulnerabilities to application owners, typically offering rewards for responsible disclosure -- a distinct threat intelligence source from feeds or reports.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Public Threat Intelligence Feeds are freely available real-time data streams (IOCs like malicious IPs/URLs/hashes/domains) -- a different source type than a researcher directly reporting a vulnerability through a reward program.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Private Threat Intelligence Feeds are paid services from cybersecurity firms offering targeted/in-depth data (often via ISACs) -- not the researcher-reward disclosure mechanism described, which is a Bounty Program.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Third-party Reports and Logs offer additional context/data on specific threats or incidents generally -- a broader category, not specifically the researcher-reward vulnerability disclosure mechanism (Bounty Programs).
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 28: Monitoring and Response
questions.explanation: Threat Intelligence Sources include Threat Intelligence Feeds (Public -- free, or Private -- paid/targeted, often via ISACs), CVE (standardized vulnerability identifiers), Bounty Programs (reward researchers for responsible vulnerability disclosure), and Third-party Reports and Logs (additional context on specific threats/incidents).

questions.question: A Windows administrator needs to review the log that specifically contains information about events generated during the operating system's installation process, as distinct from the log that aggregates entries forwarded from remote machines when centralized logging is enabled. Which two Windows log types are these, respectively?
questions.option_a: Setup (installation events); Forwarded event logs (aggregates from remote machines)
questions.option_b: Forwarded event logs (installation events); Setup (aggregates from remote machines)
questions.option_c: System (installation events); Application (aggregates from remote machines)
questions.option_d: Security (installation events); System (aggregates from remote machines)
questions.rationale_a: Correct. The Setup log contains information on events generated during the installation of the OS; Forwarded event logs aggregate logs from remote machines if centralized logging is enabled -- two of the five Windows log types alongside Security, Application, and System.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. This reverses the two -- Setup is the installation-events log, and Forwarded event logs is the remote-aggregation log, not the other way around.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. The System log records events related to the system's hardware/software (failures, driver errors), and Application log captures application-related events -- neither is the OS-installation-specific log (Setup) or the remote-log-aggregation log (Forwarded event logs).
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. The Security log tracks authentication events (logins), and System records hardware/software events -- neither matches the installation-events (Setup) or remote-aggregation (Forwarded event logs) roles described.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 28: Monitoring and Response
questions.explanation: Windows has 5 log types: Security (authentication events -- successful/failed logins), Application (application-related events), System (hardware/software events -- failures, driver errors), Setup (OS installation events), and Forwarded event logs (aggregated logs from remote machines when centralized logging is enabled).

questions.question: A cloud security tool continuously monitors an organization's cloud environments to identify misconfigurations or security risks, providing remediation recommendations based on detected issues. Which tool category is this, and which specific tool is named as an example?
questions.option_a: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM); AWS Security Hub
questions.option_c: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM); Suricata
questions.option_d: Data Loss Prevention (DLP); AWS Security Hub
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tools monitor cloud environments to identify misconfigurations or security risks, continuously monitoring and providing remediation recommendations -- AWS Security Hub is the specifically named example tool.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Behavior Baselines and Analytics establish normal activity patterns for networks/systems/users/applications (using tools like Snort/Suricata for network traffic monitoring) -- a different monitoring focus than cloud misconfiguration detection (CSPM).
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. SIEM collects/analyzes/correlates security event data from various sources broadly -- a different scope than CSPM's specific focus on cloud environment misconfigurations, and Suricata is a network intrusion detection tool, not a SIEM.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. DLP Tools protect against data loss/exfiltration -- a different function than continuously monitoring cloud environments for misconfigurations (CSPM), and AWS Security Hub is specifically the CSPM example, not a DLP tool.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 28: Monitoring and Response
questions.explanation: CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) tools continuously monitor cloud environments for misconfigurations/security risks and provide remediation recommendations -- AWS Security Hub is the named example -- distinct from Behavior Baselines/Analytics (Snort/Suricata for network traffic) and general SIEM platforms.

questions.question: A security team uses Snort and Suricata to establish what normal network traffic patterns look like over time, so they can later identify unusual data flows or unexpected connections. Which behavior baseline category is this, and which other three categories exist alongside it?
questions.option_a: Network baselines (Snort, Suricata); alongside Systems, Users, and Applications and Services baselines
questions.option_b: Systems baselines (Snort, Suricata); alongside Network, Users, and Applications and Services baselines
questions.option_c: Users baselines (Snort, Suricata); alongside Network, Systems, and Applications and Services baselines
questions.option_d: Applications and Services baselines (Snort, Suricata); alongside Network, Systems, and Users baselines
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Network baselines track typical traffic patterns to identify unusual data flows or connections, using tools like Snort and Suricata -- alongside Systems baselines (monitoring CPU/memory usage for anomalies), Users baselines (identifying deviations from normal user actions), and Applications and Services baselines (detecting anomalies in service usage or response times).
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Systems baselines monitor regular system RESOURCE usage (CPU, memory) for anomalies -- not the network TRAFFIC pattern monitoring done with Snort/Suricata, which is specifically the Network baseline category.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Users baselines identify deviations from normal USER actions (unusual login times, sensitive data access) -- not network traffic monitoring with Snort/Suricata, which is the Network category.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Applications and Services baselines detect anomalies in service usage or response times -- not network traffic pattern monitoring with Snort/Suricata, which is specifically the Network category.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 28: Monitoring and Response
questions.explanation: Behavior Baselines and Analytics establish normal patterns across four areas: Network (traffic patterns, via Snort/Suricata), Systems (CPU/memory usage anomalies), Users (deviations from normal actions like login times or sensitive data access), and Applications and Services (anomalies in usage or response times).

questions.question: A SIEM platform breaks down raw, unstructured event data into a structured format so analysts can more easily search and analyze it, while separately filtering out repeated alerts for the same underlying event to reduce alert noise. Which two SIEM concepts are these, respectively?
questions.option_a: Event parsing (structuring raw data); Event duplication (filtering repeated alerts)
questions.option_b: Event duplication (structuring raw data); Event parsing (filtering repeated alerts)
questions.option_c: Event false positives (structuring raw data); Event false negatives (filtering repeated alerts)
questions.option_d: Retention (structuring raw data); Non-reporting devices (filtering repeated alerts)
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Event parsing is the process of breaking down raw event data into structured formats for easier analysis; Event duplication filters out repeated alerts to reduce noise and enable focus on unique incidents -- two distinct SIEM data-processing functions.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. This reverses the two -- Event parsing is the structuring function, and Event duplication is the repeated-alert filtering function, not the other way around.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Event false positives (benign activity mistakenly flagged) and event false negatives (real threats undetected) describe DETECTION ACCURACY problems, not the structuring (parsing) or noise-reduction (duplication filtering) functions described.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Retention determines how long event data is stored, and Non-reporting devices are endpoints failing to send data -- neither matches the raw-data-structuring (parsing) or repeated-alert-filtering (duplication) functions described.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 28: Monitoring and Response
questions.explanation: SIEM processing includes Event parsing (structuring raw event data for analysis), Event duplication (filtering repeated alerts to reduce noise), Event false positives (benign activity wrongly flagged), and Event false negatives (real threats undetected) -- distinct functions within the broader SIEM pipeline of Collecting, Analyzing, and Responding.

questions.question: An analyst notices an attacker maintaining communications with a compromised host via DNS tunneling to remotely control malware and exfiltrate data, while the connection channel itself is encrypted to evade security tools. Which Indicator of Attack category is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Command and Control (C2) is the method by which attackers maintain communications with compromised systems, allowing them to control malware or exfiltrate data remotely -- using techniques like DNS Tunneling or connecting to malicious servers, with the channel often encrypted or concealed to evade security tools.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Persistence allows attackers to maintain access even after detection (creating admin accounts, installing backdoors, modifying settings) -- a different indicator focused on maintaining a foothold, not the communication channel itself (C2).
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Initial Access is the FIRST step attackers take to penetrate a network (phishing, exploiting vulnerabilities, stolen credentials) -- an earlier stage than the ongoing remote-control communication described (C2).
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Exfiltration is the act of stealing sensitive data and transmitting it outside the network -- while C2 can enable exfiltration, the specific DESCRIBED indicator (maintaining remote-control communications) is C2 itself, not the data-theft act.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: Indicators of Attack include Initial Access (first network penetration), Privilege Escalation, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration (stealing/transmitting data out), Command and Control (C2 -- maintaining remote communications via DNS tunneling or malicious servers, often encrypted/concealed), and Persistence (maintaining access after detection via new accounts, backdoors, or settings changes).

questions.question: A defensive team collects information about system vulnerabilities, user privileges, and critical assets specifically by analyzing an attacker's efforts to gather information WITHIN the network they've already breached. Which behavior and data analysis activity is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Internal Reconnaissance enables the identification of attacker efforts to gather information within a network -- collecting things like system vulnerabilities, user privileges, and critical assets -- observed through analyzing network logs, unusual scanning activity, and anomalous access.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Hypothesis-based Searches are driven by specific assumptions about how an attacker MIGHT operate, using available intelligence and knowledge of common attack techniques -- a proactive search approach, not specifically the observation of an attacker's own internal reconnaissance activity.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. User Behavior Analytics (UBA) monitors and flags unusual USER actions over time -- a different focus than identifying an attacker's internal information-gathering efforts specifically.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Adversary Emulation Engagements simulate attacker behavior to TEST defenses proactively -- not the observation/identification of an actual attacker's internal reconnaissance activity that's already occurring.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: Internal Reconnaissance identifies an attacker's efforts to gather information (system vulnerabilities, user privileges, critical assets) within an already-breached network -- observed via network log analysis, unusual scanning activity detection, and anomalous access observation, part of the assume-breach Threat Hunting exercise.

questions.question: A threat hunter, lacking a specific incident to investigate, instead starts with a specific assumption about how a particular type of attacker might operate within the network, using available intelligence and knowledge of common attack techniques to guide the search -- an approach that can also help detect APTs. Which threat-hunting activity is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Hypothesis-based Searches are driven by specific assumptions or scenarios about how an attacker might operate within the network, using available intelligence and knowledge of common attack techniques -- this approach can also help detect Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs).
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Internal Reconnaissance identifies an ALREADY-OCCURRING attacker's information-gathering efforts within the network -- not a hunter's own proactive, assumption-driven search approach.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. UBA monitors user actions and flags unusual behavior over time -- a data-analysis technique, not the assumption-driven search methodology (Hypothesis-based Searches) described.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Adversary Emulation Engagements simulate real-world attacker behavior to test defenses -- an active testing exercise, not a passive, assumption-driven search through existing network data.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: Hypothesis-based Searches are driven by specific assumptions about attacker behavior, using available intelligence and common attack technique knowledge -- useful for detecting APTs -- distinct from Internal Reconnaissance (observing an attacker's actual info-gathering) and User Behavior Analytics (monitoring user action patterns over time).

questions.question: A security team wants to simulate real-world attacker behavior -- including lateral movement, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration -- specifically to reveal how well current security measures actually work against known threats. Which internal intelligence source activity is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Adversary Emulation Engagements simulate real-world attacker behavior within the network -- using tools that simulate lateral movement, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration -- specifically to reveal how well current security measures work against known threats.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Honeypots are decoy systems set up to attract and detect real attackers by mimicking valuable assets -- a passive detection tool, not an active simulation of attacker behavior to test existing defenses.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Honeynets are networks of honeypots providing intelligence about how REAL attackers escalate/pivot/extract data -- observing genuine attacker behavior on decoys, not deliberately simulating attacker behavior against real production defenses.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Internal Reconnaissance identifies an actual attacker's information-gathering efforts within an already-breached network -- observing real attacker activity, not a deliberate simulation exercise to test defenses.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: Adversary Emulation Engagements simulate real-world attacker behavior (lateral movement, privilege escalation, data exfiltration) within the network specifically to reveal how well current security measures work against known threats -- an active testing exercise, distinct from passive detection tools like Honeypots/Honeynets or observation of real attacker Internal Reconnaissance.

questions.question: A threat intelligence analyst uses tools like Maltego and Shodan to collect publicly available information from websites and forums, including monitoring threat actor forums, darknet marketplaces, and public exploit databases, in order to spot emerging threats. Which external intelligence source is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. OSINT includes collecting publicly available information from websites or forums to spot emerging threats, using tools like Maltego and Shodan, and can include monitoring threat actor forums, darknet marketplaces, and public exploit databases.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. ISACs provide threat intelligence and collaboration among industries (threat reports, alerts, best practices) -- a structured industry-collaboration mechanism, not the broad public-information-gathering activity (OSINT) using tools like Maltego/Shodan.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Dark Web Monitoring specifically tracks criminal activities and potential data leaks that could signal a targeted attack -- a narrower, specialized activity within the broader OSINT umbrella (which also includes darknet marketplace monitoring, per the source material, alongside forums and exploit databases).
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. TIPs (Threat Intelligence Platforms) gather, analyze, and distribute threat data using tools like Recorded Future, FireEye, or CrowdStrike -- a platform/tooling category, not specifically the OSINT collection activity itself.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: OSINT collects publicly available information (via tools like Maltego and Shodan) from websites, forums, threat actor forums, darknet marketplaces, and public exploit databases to spot emerging threats -- one of several External Intelligence Sources alongside ISACs (industry collaboration), Dark Web Monitoring (criminal activity/leak tracking), and TIPs (aggregation platforms).

questions.question: A cybersecurity firm wants a customizable, flexible threat intelligence platform they can tailor extensively to their specific environment, as opposed to one offering premium, professionally curated intelligence out of the box. Which two platform types are these, respectively?
questions.option_a: Open-Source Platforms (flexible customization); Proprietary Platforms (premium, curated intelligence)
questions.option_b: Proprietary Platforms (flexible customization); Open-Source Platforms (premium, curated intelligence)
questions.option_c: Public Threat Intelligence Feeds (flexible customization); Private Threat Intelligence Feeds (premium, curated intelligence)
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Open-Source Platforms offer flexibility in customization, while Proprietary Platforms provide premium, curated threat intelligence -- two categories of Threat Intelligence Platforms (TIPs), which gather, analyze, and distribute threat data and allow cross-referencing external intelligence with internal logs/data.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. This reverses the two -- Open-Source is the flexible/customizable option, and Proprietary is the premium/curated option, not the other way around.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Public/Private Threat Intelligence Feeds describe FEED access models (free vs. paid data streams) -- a related but distinct concept from TIP platform types (Open-Source vs. Proprietary), which describe the analysis PLATFORM itself.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. ISACs are industry collaboration bodies providing threat reports, and TIPs is the broader platform category itself -- neither matches the specific Open-Source vs. Proprietary distinction within TIPs.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: Threat Intelligence Platforms (TIPs) gather/analyze/distribute threat data and allow cross-referencing external intelligence with internal logs -- split into Open-Source Platforms (flexible customization) and Proprietary Platforms (premium, curated intelligence), with named examples including Recorded Future, FireEye, and CrowdStrike.

questions.question: A government agency and a private security vendor participate in a real-time program that enables the immediate exchange of IP addresses, file hashes, and domain names associated with cyber threats between public and private sectors. Which IoC sharing mechanism is this, as distinct from the standardized language used to represent the threat data itself?
questions.option_a: Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS); STIX is the standardized language representing the data
questions.option_b: STIX; AIS is the standardized language representing the data
questions.option_c: TAXII; STIX is the real-time public-private sharing program
questions.option_d: CVE; TAXII is the real-time public-private sharing program
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) enables the real-time sharing of cyber threat indicators (IP addresses, file hashes, domain names) between public and private sectors; STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression) is the standardized language used to represent that threat information (IOCs, vulnerabilities, attacker tactics), while TAXII provides the protocol for exchanging it.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. This reverses AIS and STIX's roles -- AIS is the real-time public-private sharing PROGRAM, and STIX is the standardized data-representation LANGUAGE, not the other way around.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. TAXII is the protocol enabling automated STIX-formatted data exchange, not itself the public-private real-time sharing program (that's AIS); STIX is the language, not a sharing program.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. CVE is a standardized vulnerability identifier (unrelated to real-time public-private IOC sharing), and TAXII is the exchange protocol, not the sharing program itself (that's AIS).
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: IoC Sharing involves STIX (standardized language representing threat data -- IOCs, vulnerabilities, attacker tactics), TAXII (the protocol for securely/automatically exchanging that STIX-formatted data), and AIS (Automated Indicator Sharing -- enables real-time IOC exchange like IPs/hashes/domains specifically between public and private sectors).

questions.question: A forensic examiner needs to recover detailed hardware-level logs and trace signals from a suspect embedded device (like an IoT sensor) using a hardware interface standard originally designed for testing and debugging. Which interface is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. JTAG (Joint Test Action Group) Interfaces are a hardware interface standard used primarily for testing and debugging embedded systems, enabling the recovery of detailed logs and trace signals at the hardware level -- directly relevant to forensic examination of specialized/embedded devices.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Host Analysis is the examination of individual endpoints to detect signs of compromise generally -- a broader endpoint-examination activity, not specifically the hardware-level debugging INTERFACE (JTAG) used to recover embedded-system trace signals.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Network Analysis scrutinizes data traffic/communication patterns within a network -- an entirely different scope than hardware-level embedded-device log recovery via a physical debugging interface.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Reverse Engineering breaks down software/hardware to understand structure/functionality/vulnerabilities generally -- JTAG is a specific hardware INTERFACE used as a tool that can support this, but the interface itself is JTAG, not 'Reverse Engineering' as a category.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 30: Indication Analysis
questions.explanation: Infrastructure Analysis includes JTAG Interfaces (hardware debugging/testing standard enabling embedded-system log/trace recovery), Host Analysis (examining individual endpoints for compromise signs, enabling isolation/cleaning), and Network Analysis (scrutinizing traffic/communication patterns for malicious activity).

questions.question: An analyst examines a suspicious photo's underlying data and discovers the device model that captured it, the exact GPS coordinates where it was taken, and details about when and what software was used to edit it. Which type of analysis is this?
questions.option_a: Metadata Analysis (specifically of Images, Audio, and Video)
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Metadata Analysis examines underlying data about files, media, or communications -- for images/audio/video specifically, this can include device models, GPS coordinates, and editing history (when and what software was used) -- exactly matching the scenario.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Infrastructure Analysis examines hardware/software/network components for vulnerabilities or compromise signs (JTAG, Host Analysis, Network Analysis) -- a different scope than examining a single image file's embedded metadata.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Volatile Storage Analysis examines temporary data (like CPU cache) lost when a system powers off -- unrelated to persistent metadata embedded within an image file.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Code Stylometry analyzes CODING STYLE for malware attribution -- an entirely different analysis type than examining an image's embedded device/location/editing metadata.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 30: Indication Analysis
questions.explanation: Metadata Analysis examines underlying data about files/media/communications: Files and Filesystems (creation/modification dates, permissions), Images/Audio/Video (device models, GPS coordinates, editing history), and Email header analysis (sender, recipient, transmission path).

questions.question: A forensic investigator examines an email's technical header to trace exactly which mail servers the message passed through on its way to the recipient, along with confirming the original sender's address. Which metadata analysis activity is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Email header analysis examines an email's sender, recipient, and transmission path -- tracing exactly which mail servers a message passed through and confirming sender/recipient identity, a specific sub-category of Metadata Analysis.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Files and Filesystems analysis reveals file creation/modification dates and permissions -- a different metadata sub-category than tracing an EMAIL's specific transmission path and sender/recipient details.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. JTAG Interface analysis is a hardware-level debugging standard for embedded systems -- unrelated to examining email header metadata.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Host Analysis examines individual endpoints for compromise signs generally -- a broader endpoint-focused activity, not the specific email-header-tracing activity described.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 30: Indication Analysis
questions.explanation: Email header analysis (a Metadata Analysis sub-category) examines the sender, recipient, and transmission path of an email -- tracing which mail servers a message passed through, alongside Files and Filesystems analysis (creation/modification dates, permissions) and Images/Audio/Video metadata (device models, GPS, editing history).

questions.question: A forensic imaging tool preserves the unused space between a file's logical end and the storage unit's actual end, along with space marked as free but not yet overwritten, and previously deleted files -- all potential sources of hidden evidence. Which three concepts describe these three evidence sources, respectively?
questions.option_a: Slack Space; Unallocated Space; Deleted Files
questions.option_b: Unallocated Space; Slack Space; Deleted Files
questions.option_c: Deleted Files; Slack Space; Unallocated Space
questions.option_d: Slack Space; Deleted Files; Unallocated Space
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Slack Space is the unused space between a file's end and the storage unit's end; Unallocated Space is space marked as available/free (but potentially containing remnants of old data) that hasn't been overwritten; Deleted Files are files removed from the visible file system but potentially still recoverable -- all three are forensic imaging concerns preserved via bit-by-bit copying.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. This swaps Slack Space and Unallocated Space's definitions -- Slack Space is specifically the gap at a file's end within its allocated storage unit, while Unallocated Space is space marked free at the filesystem level, not the other way around.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. This places Deleted Files first, but the scenario's first description (unused space between a file's end and the storage unit's end) specifically matches Slack Space, not Deleted Files.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. This swaps Deleted Files and Unallocated Space's order relative to the scenario's descriptions -- the second description (space marked free, not yet overwritten) matches Unallocated Space, not Deleted Files.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 30: Indication Analysis
questions.explanation: Forensic Imaging preserves potential evidence in Slack Space (unused space between a file's logical end and the storage unit's end), Unallocated Space (freed space not yet overwritten), and Deleted Files (removed from the visible filesystem but potentially recoverable) -- all captured via a bit-by-bit copy using tools like dd, dcfldd, or FTK Imager, always with a write blocker to preserve the original.

questions.question: A digital forensics team needs to preserve data on a suspect's hard drive so that connecting it to their analysis workstation cannot accidentally modify the original evidence. Which hardware tool specifically enables this, and what should the team do with the original device afterward?
questions.option_a: A write blocker; keep the original device in storage and work from images of that image
questions.option_b: A write blocker; immediately destroy the original device after imaging
questions.option_c: JTAG Interfaces; immediately destroy the original device after imaging
questions.option_d: Forensic Toolkit (FTK) Imager alone, with no additional hardware needed
questions.rationale_a: Correct. A write blocker prevents any modification to the original evidence device during forensic imaging; best practice is to image the original device, keep that original device in storage, and then work from images OF that image (rather than repeatedly handling the original), preserving its integrity for potential court use.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. The original device should be preserved in storage, not destroyed -- destroying it would eliminate the ability to verify the forensic copy's integrity against the original or perform additional analysis later.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. JTAG Interfaces are a hardware debugging/testing standard for embedded systems, not the write-protection tool used during forensic imaging (that's a write blocker); and again, destroying the original device is incorrect practice.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. FTK Imager is the imaging SOFTWARE tool, but a write blocker (separate hardware) is still needed to physically prevent the connected original device from being modified during the imaging process.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 30: Indication Analysis
questions.explanation: A write blocker is the hardware tool used during forensic imaging to prevent any modification to the original evidence device; the original should be preserved in storage after imaging, with subsequent analysis performed on images of that image rather than repeatedly handling the original -- a key chain-of-custody and evidence-integrity practice.

questions.question: A malware analyst examines a piece of code represented as an intermediate, platform-independent form that virtual machines can execute, distinct from the raw ones-and-zeros the computer directly runs. Which two forms are being contrasted, respectively?
questions.option_a: Byte Code (intermediate, platform-independent, VM-executable); Binary Code (raw ones-and-zeros, directly computer-executed)
questions.option_b: Binary Code (intermediate, platform-independent, VM-executable); Byte Code (raw ones-and-zeros, directly computer-executed)
questions.option_c: Disassembly (intermediate, platform-independent, VM-executable); Decompilation (raw ones-and-zeros, directly computer-executed)
questions.option_d: Decompilation (intermediate, platform-independent, VM-executable); Disassembly (raw ones-and-zeros, directly computer-executed)
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Byte Code is a low-level representation of code executable by virtual machines, acting as an intermediate form between high-level programming and machine code for platform-independent execution; Binary Code is machine-level code the computer directly executes, made up of ones and zeros.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. This reverses the two forms -- Byte Code is the intermediate, VM-executable, platform-independent form, and Binary Code is the raw, directly-executed machine code, not the other way around.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Disassembly and Decompilation are reverse-engineering TECHNIQUES (converting binary to assembly, or executable to higher-level language) -- not the underlying code FORMS (Byte Code/Binary Code) being contrasted here.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. This also confuses techniques (Decompilation/Disassembly) with code forms (Byte Code/Binary Code) -- neither technique is itself a form of code representation.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 30: Indication Analysis
questions.explanation: Byte Code (intermediate, platform-independent, VM-executable, enabling examination without original source/platform details) and Binary Code (raw machine-level ones-and-zeros, directly executed) are the two underlying code FORMS that reverse engineering techniques like Disassembly (binary -> assembly) and Decompilation (executable -> higher-level language) operate on.

questions.question: Following a data breach, an incident responder wants to restore a critical database from a secure backup copy while separately extracting key data related to the incident itself for forensic analysis. Which Event Response activity is this?
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Data Recovery and Extraction focuses on restoring lost or compromised data and extracting critical information for analysis -- specifically securing backup copies of data and extracting key incident data, matching the scenario exactly.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Timeline Reconstruction pieces together the chronological sequence of events from logs/alerts/monitoring data -- a different Event Response activity than restoring data and extracting incident-related information.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Breach Response mitigates damage, secures systems, and ensures compliance (identifying compromised accounts, resetting credentials, notifying parties) -- a broader remediation activity, distinct from the specific data-restoration/extraction task described.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Root Cause Analysis identifies the underlying reason for an incident to prevent recurrence -- a later, different activity than restoring data and extracting incident information.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 31: Incident Response
questions.explanation: Data Recovery and Extraction restores lost/compromised data (via secure backup copies) and extracts critical incident-related information for analysis -- one of three Event Response activities alongside Timeline Reconstruction (chronological event sequencing) and Breach Response (damage mitigation and compliance).

questions.question: An investigation reveals that a current employee intentionally compromised sensitive systems, and the security team cross-references badge access logs and security camera footage with system access records to build a clear picture of the suspicious activity. Which incident response process is this, and what is emphasized as critical for managing this specific threat type going forward?
questions.option_a: Attribution; a secure and effective offboarding process is critical for managing insider threats
questions.option_b: Root Cause Analysis; a secure and effective offboarding process is critical
questions.option_c: Timeline Reconstruction; frequent password rotation is critical
questions.option_d: Breach Response; frequent password rotation is critical
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Attribution is the process of identifying the source or threat actor responsible for a security breach -- insider threats occur when an internal individual intentionally or unintentionally compromises systems/data, and physical security (cameras, access control systems, badge systems) helps identify these threats, with a secure and effective offboarding process emphasized as critical for managing insider threats specifically.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Root Cause Analysis identifies the underlying REASON for an incident (misconfigurations, unpatched software, procedural failings) to prevent recurrence -- a different focus than identifying WHO was responsible (Attribution), which is what badge logs/camera cross-referencing supports.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Timeline Reconstruction pieces together the chronological sequence of events -- while related, the scenario specifically describes identifying WHO was responsible via physical security cross-referencing, which is Attribution, and the critical safeguard named is offboarding, not password rotation.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Breach Response mitigates damage and ensures compliance -- a different, broader remediation activity than the specific insider-threat identification (Attribution) described, and the source material specifically emphasizes offboarding, not password rotation, for managing insider threats.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 31: Incident Response
questions.explanation: Attribution identifies the source/threat actor behind a breach, cross-referencing data points (including physical security -- cameras, access control, badge systems) to build clarity on suspicious activity; a secure and effective offboarding process is specifically emphasized as critical for managing insider threats.

questions.question: After resolving a security incident, a team keeps asking 'why' at each level -- why did the breach happen, why wasn't it caught sooner, why did that misconfiguration exist -- and feeds its findings back into the organization's planning process to prevent a recurrence. Which process is this, and what are its typical root causes?
questions.option_a: Root Cause Analysis (RCA); misconfigurations, unpatched software, and procedural failings
questions.option_b: Attribution; misconfigurations, unpatched software, and procedural failings
questions.option_c: Timeline Reconstruction; misconfigurations, unpatched software, and procedural failings
questions.option_d: Data Recovery and Extraction; misconfigurations, unpatched software, and procedural failings
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Root Cause Analysis (RCA) identifies the underlying reason for a security incident to prevent recurrence, using an iterative 'keep asking why' approach, with findings fed back into the planning process -- typical root causes include misconfigurations, unpatched software, and procedural failings.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. Attribution identifies WHO (the source/threat actor) was responsible for a breach -- a different focus than identifying the underlying systemic REASON (misconfiguration, unpatched software, procedural failing) the incident occurred, which is RCA.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Timeline Reconstruction pieces together the CHRONOLOGICAL SEQUENCE of events -- a different activity than the iterative 'why' questioning process that identifies systemic root causes (RCA).
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. Data Recovery and Extraction restores lost data and extracts information for analysis -- an operational recovery task, not the systemic 'why did this happen' analysis process (RCA).
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 31: Incident Response
questions.explanation: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) identifies the underlying reason for an incident using an iterative 'keep asking why' approach, feeding findings back into the planning process to prevent recurrence -- typical root causes include misconfigurations, unpatched software, and procedural failings.

questions.question: A security team runs a program that actively works to identify and neutralize adversarial actions before they succeed -- for example, feeding a suspected insider threat false information to confirm and disrupt their activity. A separate program at the same organization focuses on limiting what information about operations, plans, and capabilities is unintentionally exposed to adversaries in the first place. Which two concepts are these, respectively?
questions.option_a: Counterintelligence (CI) -- proactively detects/neutralizes adversarial actions; Operational Security (OPSEC) -- reactively limits exposed information
questions.option_b: OPSEC -- proactively detects/neutralizes adversarial actions; Counterintelligence (CI) -- reactively limits exposed information
questions.option_c: Threat hunting -- proactively detects/neutralizes adversarial actions; Threat intelligence -- reactively limits exposed information
questions.option_d: Counterintelligence (CI) -- reactively limits exposed information; OPSEC -- proactively detects/neutralizes adversarial actions
questions.rationale_a: Correct. Counterintelligence (CI) is proactive -- it actively works to detect and neutralize adversarial actions (deception, sting-style disruption of a suspected threat). OPSEC is comparatively reactive by measure -- it focuses on identifying and protecting information that could be exploited if exposed, rather than actively hunting/countering the adversary itself.
questions.rationale_b: Incorrect. This reverses the two -- CI is the proactive, adversary-neutralizing discipline; OPSEC is the more reactive information-protection discipline, not the other way around.
questions.rationale_c: Incorrect. Threat hunting and threat intelligence are related security-operations activities, but the specific proactive/reactive distinction described (actively neutralizing adversarial action vs. limiting exposed operational information) is the CI vs. OPSEC distinction, not this pair.
questions.rationale_d: Incorrect. This also reverses the pairing -- CI is the proactive, action-neutralizing discipline described first in the scenario, while OPSEC is the more reactive, information-protection discipline described second.
questions.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 29: Threat-hunting
questions.explanation: Counterintelligence (CI) is proactive: it actively detects and neutralizes adversarial actions (e.g., deception operations against a suspected insider threat). OPSEC is comparatively reactive: it focuses on limiting what operational information is exposed to adversaries in the first place, rather than actively countering them.

flashcards.term: Policy vs. Procedure vs. Standard vs. Guideline
flashcards.definition: Policy: high-level principles/expectations (what's allowed). Procedure: detailed, required step-by-step instructions. Standard: specific requirements without legal-level enforcement. Guideline: flexible, recommended best practices.
flashcards.why_it_matters: This four-tier hierarchy is the foundation of nearly all governance documentation questions on the exam.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing Standard (mandatory-in-spirit but not legally enforced, uniform requirements) with Guideline (flexible, merely recommended) -- Standards carry more weight than Guidelines despite neither being law.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: COBIT: IT governance from a manager's perspective, 4 domains (Plan and Organize, Acquire and Implement, Deliver and Support, Monitor and Evaluate), 34 processes. ITIL: IT service management from an operational perspective, most widely adopted, 34 practices including information security management.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishes governance-level (COBIT) from operational service-delivery-level (ITIL) frameworks -- a common exam pairing.
flashcards.common_trap: Mixing up which framework has '34' of what -- COBIT has 34 PROCESSES across 4 domains, while ITIL has 34 PRACTICES (a different unit of structure).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: Responsible (completes the task), Accountable (final authority, typically 1 person), Consulted (advisory input sought before decisions), Informed (kept updated, not directly involved).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Clarifies decision rights and communication flow on a project -- frequently tested via 'who is X' scenario questions.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Responsible and Accountable are interchangeable -- Responsible does the work, but Accountable holds final authority over the outcome, and only one person is typically Accountable per task.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: Mapping (SAP GRC -- links processes to regulations like GDPR), Compliance Tracking (ServiceNow GRC -- audit alerts), Automation (SAP GRC -- repetitive tasks), Continuous Monitoring (Qualys -- real-time risk/compliance), Documentation (RSA Archer -- centralized policy storage).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Matching each named tool to its specific GRC feature is a common scenario-question pattern.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any GRC tool does all five features equally -- the source material ties specific named tools to specific features (e.g., Qualys for continuous monitoring, RSA Archer for documentation).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.term: Configuration Management Database (CMDB) and Configuration Items (CIs)
flashcards.definition: CMDB is the centralized database tracking Configuration Items (CIs) -- any asset/component/service needed to deliver IT services -- with details on setup, connections, and usage, updated on every configuration change.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Underpins IT change management -- knowing what's connected to what prevents unexpected outages during updates.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing a CMDB with a general asset Inventory -- Inventory is a broader hardware/software record, while a CMDB specifically tracks CI relationships and configuration state.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: Creation -> Staging (intermediate) -> Use -> Sharing -> Storage -> Archival -> Destruction, supporting Development, Testing, QA, and Production activities.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Mapping data governance controls to lifecycle stage ensures protections (encryption, access control, retention) are applied at the right point.
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting Staging is an ADDITIONAL phase (between Creation and Use), not one of the six core lifecycle stages listed first.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: A hash collision occurs when two unique inputs produce the same hash output. MD5 and SHA-1 are known to be vulnerable to this and are no longer trusted for integrity purposes; SHA-256 and SHA-3 produce unique, unpredictable hashes resistant to collisions.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Using a collision-vulnerable algorithm undermines the entire purpose of hashing for integrity verification.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any hashing algorithm is equally trustworthy for integrity checks -- MD5/SHA-1's known collision vulnerabilities specifically disqualify them from modern integrity-critical use.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: Both are types of Connected Backups. Synchronous copies data in real-time with zero delay; Asynchronous transmits backup data with a slight delay, allowing changes to accumulate first.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The choice affects recovery point objective (RPO) -- synchronous minimizes data loss but demands more bandwidth/proximity; asynchronous tolerates distance but risks losing recent changes.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing Connected/Disconnected (network-attachment status) with Synchronous/Asynchronous (timing of data transmission) -- the latter is a sub-distinction within Connected Backups specifically.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: False Acceptance Rate (FAR): unauthorized users mistakenly accepted. False Rejection Rate (FRR): legitimate users wrongfully denied. Crossover Error Rate (CER): the point where FAR equals FRR, used to benchmark biometric accuracy.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Tuning biometric sensitivity trades FAR against FRR -- the CER is the standard metric for comparing different biometric systems' overall accuracy.
flashcards.common_trap: Mixing up FAR (letting the WRONG person in) with FRR (keeping the RIGHT person out) -- they measure opposite failure directions.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: 3 copies of data, stored across 2 different media types, with 1 copy stored off-site (disconnected).
flashcards.why_it_matters: A simple, exam-testable heuristic for resilient backup design that protects against both media failure and site-wide disasters.
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting the off-site copy must also be disconnected from the production network to remain unaffected by attacks targeting production.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.term: NIST RMF vs. ISO/IEC 27005 vs. COSO ERM vs. OCTAVE vs. FAIR
flashcards.definition: NIST RMF: federal/critical-sector, supports FISMA. ISO/IEC 27005: structured info-security risk management, complements ISO 27001's ISMS. COSO ERM: aligns risk with business strategy. OCTAVE: hands-on IT-asset risk/vulnerability assessment. FAIR: quantifies risk in financial/monetary terms.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Matching each framework to its distinguishing focus (sector, strategy alignment, IT assets, or financial quantification) is a frequently tested comparison.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating FAIR and COSO ERM as similar because both touch business impact -- FAIR is specifically about monetizing risk, while COSO ERM is about strategic alignment across the whole enterprise.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: Risk Appetite: the overall amount of risk an organization will accept to pursue its goals. Risk Tolerance: the acceptable variation within that appetite boundary.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishes the strategic risk target (appetite) from the operational flexibility around it (tolerance) -- both inform control design.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating Appetite and Tolerance as synonyms -- Appetite sets the overall level, Tolerance sets how much wiggle room exists around that level.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: Due Diligence: thorough evaluation of a vendor's reliability, risk, and integrity BEFORE partnership. Due Care: continuously taking reasonable steps to prevent harm and mitigate risk AFTER partnership begins.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are legal/professional-responsibility concepts underpinning vendor risk management and can factor into liability determinations.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Due Diligence is a one-time check that also covers ongoing vigilance -- Due Care is the specifically ongoing, ADDITIONAL responsibility after the relationship starts.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: Level 1: basic hygiene (passwords, backups, logging). Level 2: intermediate (access control, config management, incident response). Level 3: full NIST SP 800-171 implementation (advanced threat protection). Level 4: proactive security (threat hunting). Level 5: optimized defenses (adaptive controls, supply chain security, cyberthreat intelligence).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Government contractors handling CUI must meet the CMMC level tied to their contract's sensitivity -- misjudging the level risks contract non-compliance.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Level 3 (NIST SP 800-171) is the highest tier -- Levels 4 and 5 add proactive threat hunting and optimized/adaptive defenses on top of it.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Level 1: over 6 million transactions/year (annual on-site QSA audit + ROC). Level 2: 1-6 million. Level 3: 20,000-1 million. Level 4: under 20,000 e-commerce or under 1 million overall. Levels 2-4 generally use a Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) instead of an on-site audit.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Determines whether a merchant needs a costly annual on-site audit or can self-assess -- a major compliance-cost distinction.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming all PCI-DSS levels require an on-site QSA audit -- only Level 1 mandates this; Levels 2-4 typically self-assess via SAQ.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: ISO 27001: establish/maintain an ISMS. ISO 27002: best practices for ISO 27001's controls. ISO 27005: information security risk management. ISO 27017: security in cloud services. ISO 27018: protecting personal data in the cloud.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Each numbered standard addresses a distinct compliance need -- citing the wrong one in documentation or an audit response is a common, avoidable error.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing ISO 27017 (cloud SERVICE security) with ISO 27018 (cloud PERSONAL DATA protection) -- they're both cloud-focused but address different protection targets.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.term: SOC 2 Type I vs. Type II vs. SOC 3
flashcards.definition: SOC 2 Type I: control DESIGN at a point in time. SOC 2 Type II: design PLUS operational effectiveness over 6-12 months. SOC 3: simplified, public-facing summary of SOC 2 findings.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Vendors often cite their SOC 2 report type as a trust signal -- knowing the difference reveals how rigorously their controls were actually tested.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating a SOC 2 Type I report as equivalent proof of ongoing operational security -- it only confirms controls were properly designed at one moment, not that they worked over time.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Identify (asset management -- SolarWinds, Lansweeper), Protect (firewalls, encryption, IAM), Detect (IDS, SIEM), Respond (IBM Resilient, CrowdStrike), Recover (Veeam, Acronis).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Provides a simple, memorable 5-stage mental model for organizing an entire cybersecurity program.
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting Identify comes first -- you can't effectively Protect, Detect, Respond to, or Recover from threats to assets you haven't first mapped/identified.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Configuration Baseline: an organization's own internal minimum security configuration standard. Benchmark (e.g., CIS Benchmarks): an external, industry-recognized reference point used to verify how well the baseline measures up.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishes an org's self-set internal standard from the external yardstick used to validate it against industry best practice.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating 'baseline' and 'benchmark' as synonyms -- baseline is what YOU set internally; benchmark is the EXTERNAL standard you compare against.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Cloud Security Alliance certification process evaluating cloud providers' security practices via a publicly accessible registry. Level 1: self-assessment. Level 2: third-party audit.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Gives customers a transparent way to compare cloud providers' security posture before choosing a vendor.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing CSA STAR's Level 1/2 (self-assessment vs. third-party audit) with PCI-DSS's Level 1-4 (transaction-volume tiers) -- both use 'Level' numbering but for entirely different purposes.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Legal Hold: preventing deletion/alteration of information that might be needed as court evidence. E-discovery: the process of searching preserved data to find case-relevant information (conducted by legal, IT, and third-party vendors).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Failing a Legal Hold obligation (allowing evidence to be deleted) can result in serious legal sanctions independent of the underlying case's merits.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming E-discovery can begin before a Legal Hold is in place -- the hold must first preserve the data so there's something intact to search.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: COPPA applies to website operators/online services directed toward children under 13 -- critically, if a product COULD be used by younger audiences, COPPA applies regardless of specific marketing intent.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A common compliance trap: apps not marketed to children can still trigger COPPA if children could plausibly use them.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming COPPA only applies if a service is deliberately marketed to children -- the actual trigger is broader, based on potential use by that age group.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.term: Awareness and Training Concepts (SET, Social Engineering, Phishing, Situational Awareness)
flashcards.definition: SET: open-source social engineering simulation tool. Social Engineering: manipulation to divulge confidential info. Phishing: fraudulent communications, a specific social engineering tactic. Situational Awareness: ongoing understanding of the threat landscape.
flashcards.why_it_matters: These form the vocabulary for security awareness training programs and their measurement tools.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating Phishing as a synonym for Social Engineering broadly -- Phishing is one specific TACTIC within the broader Social Engineering category.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: Planning and Procurement -> Deployment -> Utilization and Maintenance -> Asset Tracking -> Decommissioning and Disposal.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Ensures assets remain functional, secure, and properly retired throughout their entire lifespan, not just at acquisition.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing this with the Data Lifecycle (Creation/Use/Sharing/Storage/Archival/Destruction) -- one tracks physical/IT ASSETS, the other tracks DATA.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: System Center Configuration Manager -- tracks and manages hardware and software assets, collecting hardware details and monitoring installed software.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A concrete, named example tool for implementing the broader Inventory concept in Change and Configuration Management.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming SCCM IS the CMDB -- SCCM feeds inventory/asset data that supports building and maintaining a CMDB, but they're distinct concepts.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 2: Governance

flashcards.definition: Incident (any unplanned event affecting CIA requiring response), Sensitive Data Breach (unauthorized access to PII), Privileged Data Breach (unauthorized access to highly sensitive data like financial/health info -- mitigated via MFA/DLP/privileged account audits), Data Leak Response (identify source, contain, correct), Reporting (inadequate reporting risks prolonged exposure and legal/reputational harm).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Frames the specific vocabulary and control set for confidentiality-focused risk scenarios, distinct from integrity or availability risk.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating 'Sensitive Data Breach' and 'Privileged Data Breach' as synonyms -- Privileged Data Breach specifically involves HIGHLY sensitive data (financial/health) and has its own named control set.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: Interference (unauthorized modification -- mitigated by access controls, authentication, monitoring, backups/failover), Hashing (fixed-size fingerprint for detecting alteration), Remote Journaling (continuous transaction log transmission to a remote location), Anti-Tampering/Tamper-evident Logging (detects/alerts on unauthorized modification attempts).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Provides the specific named controls for protecting data accuracy and detecting unauthorized changes.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing Remote Journaling (continuous LOG transmission for a duplicate record) with a backup (a full data copy) -- journaling specifically preserves transaction-level history, not a complete system snapshot.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: Hot Site (fully equipped, near-immediate activation, highest cost), Warm Site (partially equipped, moderate readiness/cost), Cold Site (no pre-installed equipment, built out during disaster, slowest/cheapest), Cloud Site (cloud-based infrastructure for flexible recovery).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Choosing the right site type balances recovery time objectives against budget -- a frequently tested BC/DR planning decision.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Warm Site is just 'a slower Hot Site' -- it's specifically PARTIALLY equipped, occupying a distinct middle position rather than just a slower version of full readiness.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.term: BIA vs. Impact Analysis vs. BC/DR Testing
flashcards.definition: BIA: identifies/evaluates effects of losing Mission Essential Functions (MEFs). Impact Analysis: a 5-step process evaluating consequences of risks on operations/finance/compliance via extreme scenarios. BC/DR Testing: live/simulated drills verifying recovery strategies actually work (surfaces communication/equipment/staffing gaps).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Each activity answers a different question -- what would we lose (BIA), how bad would specific scenarios be (Impact Analysis), and does our plan actually work (Testing) -- and all three are needed together.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating BIA and Impact Analysis as the same process -- BIA is specifically MEF-focused within BC/DR planning, while Impact Analysis is a broader 5-step scenario-consequence process.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: Identification -> Assessment -> Control -> Review -- the four-stage cycle underlying all risk analysis approaches.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Provides the structural backbone that Qualitative, Quantitative, and Hybrid analysis methods all operate within.
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting Review is a distinct, ongoing final stage -- risk management is cyclical, not a one-time linear process that ends at Control.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.term: Vendor Risk vs. Subprocessor Risk vs. Supply Chain Risk
flashcards.definition: Vendor Risk: direct suppliers' potential impact (mitigated via Due Diligence pre-partnership and Due Care ongoing). Subprocessor Risk: a vendor's own subcontractors (mitigated by requiring disclosure and verifying their security practices). Supply Chain Risk: spans all stages, including both (verified via supply chain assessments and source authenticity checks).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishes direct, indirect, and end-to-end third-party risk exposure -- each requiring different verification steps.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming vetting the primary vendor (Vendor Risk) automatically covers subcontractors too -- Subprocessor Risk requires its own explicit disclosure and verification step.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 3: Risk Management

flashcards.definition: HIPAA: protects patients' sensitive health information and privacy. HITECH: builds on HIPAA, encouraging healthcare providers to adopt electronic health records (EHRs).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both work together to ensure privacy and strict rules around medical data storage/sharing -- a common compliance pairing in healthcare exam scenarios.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating HITECH as a replacement for HIPAA rather than a law that BUILDS ON it -- HITECH specifically adds EHR-adoption incentives on top of HIPAA's privacy protections.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.term: GLBA vs. SOX vs. PCI-DSS (Financial Regulations)
flashcards.definition: GLBA: protects customers' personal financial information at banks. SOX: ensures public companies maintain accurate financial records and anti-fraud controls. PCI-DSS: applies to any business handling credit card transactions (6 security goals).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Each financial regulation targets a different actor (banks, public companies, or any card-processing business) and a different risk.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming PCI-DSS only applies to banks like GLBA does -- PCI-DSS applies to ANY business handling credit card transactions, regardless of industry.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Build and maintain a secure network, maintain a vulnerability management program, continuously monitor systems, encrypt cardholder data, enforce strict access controls, maintain a robust information security policy.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A memorable checklist for any organization handling card payments, regardless of PCI-DSS processor level.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing the 6 high-level GOALS with PCI-DSS's more granular official numbered REQUIREMENTS structure -- the source material's '6 goals' framing is a simplified summary, not the full official requirement count.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: NERC-CIP: secures the systems that keep power grids running (utility company security practices). FERC: federal body overseeing/enforcing compliance across the broader energy industry.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishes a specific technical security standard (NERC-CIP) from the regulatory body enforcing broader industry compliance (FERC).
flashcards.common_trap: Treating NERC-CIP and FERC as interchangeable -- NERC-CIP is the security STANDARD, FERC is the ENFORCEMENT body overseeing the industry.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: EU regulation ensuring fair competition in digital markets. Gatekeepers: companies controlling key digital services (search engines, social networks, app stores), subject to the DMA's rules to give smaller companies a fair chance to compete.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Represents a newer category of tech-industry-specific compliance distinct from data-privacy regulations like GDPR.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing the DMA (digital market COMPETITION regulation) with GDPR (data PRIVACY regulation) -- both are EU laws but address entirely different concerns.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: 5 categories: Security (unauthorized access protection), Availability (reliability), Processing Integrity (accurate/complete processing), Confidentiality (sensitive info protection), Privacy (personal data handling).
flashcards.why_it_matters: These are the specific evaluation categories underlying any SOC 2 Type I or Type II report -- knowing them helps interpret what a SOC 2 report actually certifies.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing SOC 2's Confidentiality and Privacy criteria -- Confidentiality covers protecting sensitive info generally, while Privacy specifically covers PERSONAL data collection/storage/management practices.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Respond: contain incidents, investigate root causes, notify personnel (tools: IBM Resilient, CrowdStrike). Recover: restore lost data/services after an incident (tools: Veeam, Acronis).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Completes the NIST CSF's 5-function lifecycle alongside Identify, Protect, and Detect -- Respond and Recover specifically cover the active-incident and post-incident phases.
flashcards.common_trap: Mixing up Respond (active containment/investigation) with Recover (restoration afterward) -- Respond happens DURING the incident, Recover happens AFTER it's contained.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: COPPA: protects children under 13 (US). LGPD: Brazil's data protection law for individuals in Brazil. CCPA: California residents' rights (know what's collected, request deletion, opt out of sale).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Each privacy law has a distinct population/jurisdiction scope -- misapplying one to the wrong population is a common compliance error.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming all three grant the same rights -- CCPA specifically includes an opt-out-of-sale right that COPPA and LGPD don't frame the same way.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: External Assessment: outside consultants identify unseen weaknesses and recommend improvements (exploratory). External Audit: independent third-party auditors formally verify compliance with external regulations, results often shared with regulators/clients (formal, compliance-focused).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishes a helpful diagnostic engagement from a formal compliance-verification engagement, both performed by outside parties.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any 'outside security review' is automatically a formal Audit -- an External Assessment is exploratory and improvement-focused, not necessarily tied to formal regulatory compliance verification.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance
