flashcards.term: Export Controls and the Wassenaar Arrangement
flashcards.definition: Export Controls regulate international transfer of dual-use technologies (usable by both government and private sectors, e.g., certain firewalls). The Wassenaar Arrangement is the international agreement controlling these exports; an export license may be required.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Relevant for any security vendor or enterprise selling security technology internationally.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming export controls only apply to obviously military technology -- 'dual-use' explicitly includes everyday security technology like firewalls that also have government applications.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: NIST SP 800-84 = Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities (tabletop -> functional -> full-scale exercises). NIST SP 800-122 = Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam tests precise NIST SP number-to-topic mapping across a long list (800-53, 800-61, 800-84, 800-88, 800-122, 800-161, 800-171, CSF, RMF) -- confusing any two costs a question.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing 800-84 (testing/exercising plans) with 800-61 (the incident-handling process itself), or confusing 800-122 (PII confidentiality) with 800-88 (media sanitization) -- both pairs sound adjacent but cover different lifecycle stages.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: ISO 9001 is a Quality Management Systems (QMS) standard for consistent product/service quality and process improvement. ISO/IEC 27001 is the Information Security Management System (ISMS) standard for security program certification.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are 'ISO certifications' an organization might advertise, but only 27001 speaks to information security -- 9001 certification implies nothing about security controls.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any ISO certification implies security compliance -- ISO covers hundreds of unrelated standards (quality, environmental management, food safety), and only the 27000-series addresses information security.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation is formally published as the international standard ISO/IEC 15408 -- they are the same framework, not two separate ones.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Unlike most 'framework vs. ISO number' pairs (which ARE distinct), this is the one case where the named framework and the ISO standard number refer to identical content.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating Common Criteria and ISO/IEC 15408 as competing or alternative evaluation frameworks when they are literally the same standard under two names.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Trusted Hardware/Software

flashcards.definition: The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) is the standards body that defines and governs SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3 report requirements and the Trust Service Criteria SOC 2 evaluates against.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Knowing AICPA is the issuing body (not an ISO-style international standards organization) clarifies why SOC reports are audit attestations by CPA firms, not certifications like ISO 27001.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming SOC reports are ISO-style certifications issued by an international standards body -- SOC reports are CPA-firm audit attestations governed by AICPA standards, a fundamentally different mechanism than ISO certification.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 4: Compliance

flashcards.definition: Circuit-level Proxy: operates at the session layer. Application-level Proxy: inspects traffic at the application layer (deepest). Kernel Proxy: filters across multiple OSI layers with minimal delay.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios describing a specific OSI layer of inspection point directly to one of these three proxy variants.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming all proxy firewalls provide the same depth of inspection -- Application-level provides the deepest content-aware filtering, while Circuit-level only operates at the session layer.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 5: Resilient System Design

flashcards.definition: IDS (Network/Host/Wireless) detects and alerts on malicious activity WITHOUT taking action. IPS (Network/Host/Wireless) actively blocks/prevents threats, with Network IPS placed directly inline with traffic.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A foundational, heavily tested distinction -- detection-only vs. active-blocking -- that also determines physical placement (IPS must be inline).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming an IDS can block traffic just because it's monitoring it -- by definition, IDS only detects/alerts; only an IPS takes blocking action.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 5: Resilient System Design

flashcards.definition: Forward/Transparent Proxy: edge-positioned, regulates OUTBOUND traffic per acceptable use policy. Reverse Proxy: edge-positioned, handles INBOUND connections (completes TCP handshake, connects to origin server), offering caching, traffic scrubbing, IP masking, and load balancing.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both proxies sit at the network edge but handle opposite traffic directions -- a frequently tested contrast, and an API Gateway acting as a proxy is specifically acting as a Reverse Proxy.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing which proxy handles which direction -- Forward/Transparent = outbound (users leaving the network); Reverse = inbound (external users reaching internal services).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 5: Resilient System Design

flashcards.definition: Round Robin (sequential distribution), Least Connections (fewest active connections gets next request), IP Hashing (maps a client IP consistently to one server -- supports session persistence).
flashcards.why_it_matters: IP Hashing is the specific method to recall when a scenario requires the SAME client to always reach the SAME server.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Round Robin provides session consistency -- it distributes purely sequentially with no regard for which server a client previously used.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 5: Resilient System Design

flashcards.definition: Scaling Up (vertical): adds resources to an existing machine, hardware-capacity-limited. Scaling Out (horizontal): partitions data across multiple servers/databases, virtually limitless, built-in redundancy, but requires Stateless Applications.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A key exam trap: Scaling Out's benefits (redundancy, limitless growth, per-use cost) come with the specific architectural cost of requiring statelessness.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Scaling Out works with any application design -- it specifically requires Stateless Applications, since session data can't be reliably tied to one server across a horizontally distributed system.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 5: Resilient System Design

flashcards.definition: Full: complete copy, slow/storage-heavy. Incremental: changes since last backup of any type, fast but multi-file restore. Differential: all changes since last FULL backup. Synthetic Full: administratively combines full+incremental into a new complete backup without recopying everything.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A classic exam matrix -- know the precise definition of each backup type, especially Differential (since-last-FULL) vs. Incremental (since-last-backup-of-any-type).
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing Differential (measured from the last full backup) with Incremental (measured from the last backup, full or incremental) -- this changes both restore speed and file count needed.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 5: Resilient System Design

flashcards.definition: Tabletop (discussion/walkthrough) < Simulation (mock disaster, no production impact) < Parallel (backups run alongside production) < Full Interruption (production actually taken offline, real failover).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Ordering these by realism/risk helps answer 'which test type is needed without disrupting production' vs. 'which test proves real failover capability.'
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Simulation and Full Interruption are interchangeable because both involve a 'disaster' scenario -- only Full Interruption actually takes production systems offline.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 5: Resilient System Design

flashcards.definition: Data at rest: symmetric encryption (AES-256), TDE, BitLocker/FileVault. Data in transit: TLS, IPsec, SSH/SFTP. Data in use: memory encryption, RBAC/ABAC, data masking, secure enclaves (Intel SGX).
flashcards.why_it_matters: A foundational CAS-005 concept -- match the protection technology to the correct data state (rest/transit/use).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming TLS or IPsec protects data at rest -- those specifically protect data IN TRANSIT; data at rest needs disk/database-level encryption like TDE or BitLocker/FileVault.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 6: Secure Architecture Design

flashcards.definition: Government/Military: Unclassified, Confidential, Secret (SIPRNet), Top Secret -- relies on physical separation. Commercial/Business: Public, Private, Internal, Restricted, Confidential -- relies on logical isolation.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios naming specific classification labels point to one model or the other -- and SIPRNet is a specific, testable detail for the Secret level.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Commercial/Business classification uses physical network separation like SIPRNet -- it explicitly relies on logical isolation instead.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 6: Secure Architecture Design

flashcards.definition: Alert (logs/notifies, still allows transfer) -> Block (stops transfer) -> Quarantine (alert + block + removes access) -> Tombstone (alert + block + quarantine + replaces file with violation message).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Know the exact escalation order and that Tombstone is the most severe, uniquely replacing the file itself.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Block is the most severe DLP action -- Quarantine and Tombstone both go further by also removing access and/or replacing the file.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 6: Secure Architecture Design

flashcards.definition: IaaS: rent virtualized infrastructure, install your own OS and build custom apps. PaaS: complete development platform, infrastructure AND OS/dev tools provided. SaaS: ready-to-use hosted applications (email, CRM).
flashcards.why_it_matters: A classic exam matrix testing which service model gives you OS-level control (IaaS) versus a ready dev platform (PaaS) versus a finished application (SaaS).
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing PaaS (platform with dev tools ready) with IaaS (raw infrastructure where you install your own OS) -- the key differentiator is how much of the stack you manage yourself.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 6: Secure Architecture Design

flashcards.term: Control Effectiveness: Metrics, Scanning, and Assessments
flashcards.definition: Metrics: incident response time, vulnerabilities mitigated, incident frequency, patch %, false positive rate. Scanning: detecting outdated software/misconfigured firewalls/open ports. Assessments: audits, penetration testing (including Time to Detect and Respond), compliance checks, control implementation %.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Know which specific metric (like Time to Detect and Respond) belongs to which broader assessment category (penetration testing specifically).
flashcards.common_trap: Treating all control-effectiveness figures as interchangeable 'metrics' -- Scanning and Assessments are distinct activity categories from the Metrics list itself.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 6: Secure Architecture Design

flashcards.term: MAC vs. DAC vs. RBAC(rule) vs. ABAC
flashcards.definition: MAC: static classification labels, admin-only control (SELinux, gov/mil). DAC: resource owner controls access (default in Windows/Linux). Rule-Based Access Control: admin-configured rules/conditions (e.g., firewall ACLs). ABAC: dynamic, multi-attribute (role+department+location).
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam frequently tests matching a described access-granting mechanism to the correct one of these four models -- know the defining trait of each.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing 'Role-Based Access Control' with 'Rule-Based Access Control' -- the notes explicitly cover both role-based (job-function-driven) and the separate rule/condition-based model; don't conflate the two just because both abbreviate to RBAC.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 8: Access, Authentication, Authorization

flashcards.definition: Login -> KDC verifies identity -> issues Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) -> client presents TGT to KDC's Ticket Granting Service (TGS) -> TGS issues a service ticket -> client presents service ticket to the service (SP) for access, no re-authentication needed.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Kerberos's specific TGT-then-service-ticket flow (used heavily in Active Directory) is a frequently tested sequencing question.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming a single ticket handles everything -- Kerberos specifically uses a TWO-step ticket process (TGT first, then a per-service ticket from the TGS).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 8: Access, Authentication, Authorization

flashcards.definition: Policy Decision Point (PDP): evaluates whether an access request complies with policy (location, device, time). Policy Enforcement Point (PEP): the gatekeeper that actually allows or blocks access based on the PDP's decision.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A foundational Zero Trust/access-control vocabulary pair -- 'decides' (PDP) versus 'enforces' (PEP) is a very common exam discriminator.
flashcards.common_trap: Reversing PDP and PEP's roles -- PDP decides, PEP enforces; remembering 'Decision' and 'Enforcement' in the full names helps keep them straight.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 8: Access, Authentication, Authorization

flashcards.definition: PRI code = (Facility number x 8) + Severity level. Severity ranges from 0 (Emergency, most severe) to 7 (Debugging Information, least severe).
flashcards.why_it_matters: A specific, calculable exam fact -- expect a scenario giving facility and severity numbers and asking you to compute or interpret the resulting PRI code.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming severity 0 is the LEAST severe -- it's actually the MOST severe (Emergency); severity 7 (Debugging) is the least urgent.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 8: Access, Authentication, Authorization

flashcards.definition: Bastion Host: a hardened server placed in a vulnerable/exposed area to withstand external attacks generally. Jump Box: similar hardened concept, but specifically used to provide secure administrative access to internal systems.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are hardened, exposed-area devices, but the Jump Box's defining trait is its specific purpose: secure ADMIN access, not general attack resistance.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating these as fully identical -- Jump Box is a specialized application of the bastion host concept, specifically for administrative access.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 9: Zero Trust Design

flashcards.definition: Client-Server VPN: individual device to central server (IPsec/TLS). Site-to-Site VPN: whole networks connected at router level (IPsec). Always-On VPN: continuously active, auto-connects on power-on, enforces policy regardless of location, integrates MFA/NAC.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Match the described scope (one device, whole network, or continuous/location-independent) to the correct VPN architecture.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Site-to-Site VPN is for individual remote users -- it specifically connects entire networks/branch offices at the router level, not individual client devices.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 9: Zero Trust Design

flashcards.definition: Control Plane: routing/traffic management decisions. Data Plane: actually moves traffic between devices. Management Plane: administrative oversight and configuration changes.
flashcards.why_it_matters: SD-WAN and SASE both build on this SDN foundation, so knowing the three planes clearly helps distinguish SDN from its more specialized descendants.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing the Control Plane (decides HOW to route) with the Data Plane (actually MOVES the traffic) -- a very common mix-up in networking exam questions generally.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 9: Zero Trust Design

flashcards.definition: SDN: software controls network functions via Control/Data/Management planes. SD-WAN: builds on SDN specifically for wide-area, multi-site connections with centralized cloud control. SASE: combines networking AND security (firewalls, secure web gateways, ZTNA) into one cloud-based service.
flashcards.why_it_matters: These three build on each other in scope -- SDN (general software control) -> SD-WAN (wide-area specialization) -> SASE (adds integrated security) -- a common exam progression to test.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming SASE is just another name for SD-WAN -- SASE specifically differentiates itself by integrating SECURITY tools (firewalls, secure web gateways, ZTNA) alongside networking, not just optimizing connectivity.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 9: Zero Trust Design

flashcards.definition: Authentication (OAuth/API keys/JWTs) -> Authorization (RBAC/ABAC) -> Input Validation (format/business rules) -> Security Measures (SQL injection/buffer overflow checks).
flashcards.why_it_matters: A precise, sequence-based exam fact -- questions may ask 'what comes first' or 'what comes after authorization.'
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming input validation or security checks happen before authentication -- identity must be established first, since authorization and subsequent checks depend on knowing who is making the request.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 9: Zero Trust Design

flashcards.definition: Asset Identification: build the inventory (Nmap/Nessus, SCCM, AWS Asset Manager/Azure Resource Manager, EDR). Asset Management: ongoing monitoring/maintenance (WSUS, Ansible/Puppet/Chef, Intune, ServiceNow). Asset Attestation: verify security posture/compliance (EDR, SIEM, Tenable/Qualys).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Three sequential stages of Asset Control -- know which named tools belong to which stage, since scenario questions often name a specific tool.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming all these tools are interchangeable across the three stages -- each stage has its own distinct named toolset in the source material (e.g., WSUS is Management, not Identification).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 9: Zero Trust Design

flashcards.definition: Framework defining which cloud security tasks the provider handles versus which the client handles.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Determines where the customer's own security obligations begin, especially for IAM configuration and data protection.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming the cloud provider secures everything -- Customer Specific controls (like IAM policy configuration) remain entirely the client's job regardless of service model.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 18: Cloud Security

flashcards.definition: A security control point between cloud users and cloud applications that enforces policy, monitors usage, detects threats, and validates compliance.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Provides centralized visibility and control over cloud usage that individual SaaS apps don't offer on their own.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing API-based (no traffic rerouting, seamless) with proxy-based (inline, real-time inspection) deployment -- they have very different user-experience and coverage tradeoffs.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 18: Cloud Security

flashcards.definition: Residual data that remains on storage devices after deletion, a concern when VMs, containers, or volumes are moved or removed.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Attackers or new tenants on shared infrastructure could recover 'deleted' sensitive data if remanence isn't addressed.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming a simple delete/format is sufficient -- proper mitigation requires cryptographic erasure or physical destruction.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 18: Cloud Security

flashcards.definition: Unauthorized cloud services or applications used by employees without IT's knowledge or approval.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Creates data leakage and compliance risk because these tools typically lack sanctioned security controls.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating it purely as a policy violation -- the recommended remediation is detection via monitoring plus a path to an approved alternative, not just blocking.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 18: Cloud Security

flashcards.definition: Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool that provisions cloud infrastructure; Ansible is an agentless configuration-management/deployment tool using YAML playbooks.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are common exam distinctions between provisioning infrastructure versus configuring/deploying onto it.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming both tools do the same job -- Terraform provisions, Ansible configures and deploys, and Ansible needs no agent software installed.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 18: Cloud Security

flashcards.definition: Running application code (functions) without managing underlying infrastructure; functions are lightweight, stateless, and scale automatically.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Shifts security focus to code and function permissions rather than server hardening, since there's no OS to patch.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming 'serverless' means no infrastructure exists at all -- the provider still manages compute/storage/networking resources behind the scenes.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 18: Cloud Security

flashcards.definition: Source code integration -> automated testing (security, performance, functional) -> build and deployment -> monitoring and feedback.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Knowing the phase order helps identify where a given security control (like a security scan) fits in the pipeline.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing Continuous Integration (merging + testing) with Continuous Deployment (automatically pushing tested code to production) -- they're sequential, distinct phases.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 18: Cloud Security

flashcards.definition: Integrates all necessary electronics into a single chip, achieving very low power consumption; examples include Raspberry Pi, Roku, and smartphones.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Requires security embedded at the hardware level since the entire system is one integrated unit, vulnerable to both physical and cyber threats.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing SoC with a generic embedded system -- SoC specifically means all components live on a single chip.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 19: Specialized System Security

flashcards.definition: Zigbee uses 2.4 GHz (faster transfer, more devices, good for bigger systems); Z-Wave uses ~900 MHz (better range and wall penetration, more reliable in larger homes/buildings).
flashcards.why_it_matters: A classic exam pairing testing whether you know which frequency trades speed/device-count for range/penetration.
flashcards.common_trap: Mixing up which protocol favors range versus device density -- Z-Wave = range (lower frequency), Zigbee = speed/devices (higher frequency).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 19: Specialized System Security

flashcards.definition: ICS manages industrial processes broadly; SCADA is a subset of ICS for remote monitoring/control across wide geographic areas; DCS interconnects multiple ICS for large-scale operational efficiency.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam questions often test which term is the broadest category versus which is geographically/architecturally specific.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating SCADA and ICS as synonyms -- SCADA is specifically the remote, wide-area monitoring subset of the broader ICS category.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 19: Specialized System Security

flashcards.definition: Obsolete (outdated, incompatible architecture), Unsupported (no more vendor updates/patches), Unable to Secure (can't support modern defenses like encryption/MFA), Highly Constrained (limited processing/memory/connectivity).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Each characteristic implies a different remediation: Unsupported needs compensating controls or replacement planning; Highly Constrained limits what security can even be layered on.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating all four as interchangeable -- 'obsolete' (outdated tech) is distinct from 'unsupported' (no vendor patches), even though both often occur together.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 19: Specialized System Security

flashcards.definition: Batch processing collects data over a fixed period (e.g., eight hours) and processes it in bulk; stream processing analyzes data in near real-time.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The choice affects how quickly a SOC can detect and respond to threats in specialized-system environments.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming batch processing is obsolete and never used -- it was common historically and may still appear in exam scenarios describing legacy pipelines.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 19: Specialized System Security

flashcards.definition: Tools that monitor and secure databases by detecting unauthorized access and suspicious activity, using interception-based (network sniffing), memory-based (memory scraping), and log-based (reading system tables/logs) methods.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Provides a database-specific layer of monitoring beyond general network or endpoint tools.
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting there are three distinct DAM methods (interception, memory, log-based) rather than one single detection approach.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 19: Specialized System Security

flashcards.definition: Safety compliance standard covering functional safety in electronic systems, including fail-safes and risk-reduction measures.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to OT/ICS environments where a safety failure could cause physical harm, not just data loss.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing IEC 61508 (functional/physical safety standard) with data-protection regulations like GDPR or HIPAA -- it addresses accident prevention, not data privacy.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 19: Specialized System Security

flashcards.definition: Packet filtering firewalls inspect only the packet header; stateful firewalls track the state of active connections.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishing these two firewall types by their inspection depth is a recurring exam distinction.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming both firewall types track connection state -- only stateful firewalls do.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: A proxy firewall that filters traffic across multiple OSI model layers with minimal delay, balancing security and performance.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Represents the performance-optimized evolution of proxy firewalls compared to circuit-level and application-level proxies.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing it with a circuit-level proxy, which operates only at the session layer.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Signature-based detection recognizes known attack patterns; anomaly-based detection flags deviations from an established baseline.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Signature-based methods miss novel/zero-day attacks that anomaly-based methods can catch, and vice versa for false positives.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming signature-based detection can catch unknown/zero-day attacks -- it can only match known patterns.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Active TAPs physically interrupt and regenerate the monitored signal and can continue capturing during network failures; passive TAPs require no power but pass all traffic including malformed packets.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Choosing the wrong TAP type can mean losing visibility during an outage (passive) or introducing a single point of failure (active).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming passive TAPs are always superior because they require no power -- they cannot filter malformed packets and lack active TAP's failure resilience.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable downtime; Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
flashcards.why_it_matters: These two metrics drive the entire backup and failover architecture decision for a DR plan.
flashcards.common_trap: Swapping RTO and RPO's definitions -- RTO is about time-to-restore, RPO is about how much data can be lost.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Scaling up (vertical) adds resources to an existing machine; scaling out (horizontal) partitions data across multiple databases, requiring a stateless application.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Horizontal scaling offers virtually limitless, per-use-cost growth with built-in redundancy, while vertical scaling is bounded by a single machine's hardware capacity.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming horizontal scaling works with stateful applications that store session data on a single server -- it requires stateless application design.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Allowlists block all data except what is explicitly allowed (default-deny); denylists allow all data unless specifically denied (default-allow).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Choosing the wrong default posture can either block legitimate business traffic or let unauthorized data slip through undetected.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming an allowlist and denylist are interchangeable terms for the same restrictive posture -- they represent opposite default behaviors.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Alert (log + notify, allow transfer) -> Block (stop transfer) -> Quarantine (alert + block + remove access) -> Tombstone (all of the above + replace file with violation message).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Knowing the escalation order helps configure DLP policies proportional to data sensitivity.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Block is the most severe action -- Tombstone is more severe, replacing the file entirely.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: IaaS: rent virtualized infrastructure and manage your own OS. PaaS: complete development platform with infrastructure and OS tools included. SaaS: ready-to-use hosted applications.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Choosing the wrong service model affects how much of the security stack the organization is responsible for managing.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing PaaS (development platform) with IaaS (raw infrastructure) -- PaaS already includes the OS-level development tooling.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Unclassified (no risk if disclosed) -> Confidential (authorized/NDA only) -> Secret (stricter, SIPRNet-eligible) -> Top Secret (grave danger if disclosed).
flashcards.why_it_matters: This four-tier model underlies access decisions and system isolation requirements like SIPRNet for Secret-level data.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Confidential is the most restrictive level in the government model -- Top Secret is more restrictive.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Rule-Based Access Control uses predefined rules/conditions (e.g., firewall ACLs), configured by administrators. Role-Based Access Control assigns users to roles that determine resource access.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both share the acronym RBAC on the exam, making this one of the most commonly confused pairs in access control.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming 'RBAC' always refers to Role-Based Access Control -- context determines which model is meant.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: A physical security control using an interlocking chamber where only one door can be open at a time, specifically to prevent tailgating.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Directly addresses the tailgating attack vector where an unauthorized person follows an authorized person into a secure area.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing a mantrap with a simple keypad entry system -- the mantrap's defining feature is the interlocking dual-door chamber, not just authentication.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: PRI code = (Facility number x 8) + Severity level. Severity ranges from 0 (Emergency) to 7 (Debugging Information).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Being able to calculate or interpret a PRI code is a concrete, testable skill for log analysis questions.
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting the multiplication step and just adding facility + severity directly.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: SAML uses an XML-based attestation message; JWT uses a signed JSON-based token. Both transmit authentication/authorization information between an IdP and SP.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Recognizing the underlying data format (XML vs. JSON) helps identify which protocol a given implementation is using.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming SAML and JWT are interchangeable formats -- they use different serialization (XML vs. JSON) and are often used in different ecosystems.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Control Plane (routing/traffic decisions), Data Plane (actual traffic movement between devices), Management Plane (administrative oversight and changes).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Understanding the layered SDN model clarifies where security controls and monitoring should be applied.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing the control plane (decisions) with the data plane (execution) -- the control plane decides, the data plane carries out.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Secure Access Service Edge -- combines networking and security into a single cloud-based service, integrating firewalls, secure web gateways, and Zero Trust Network Access.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Represents the convergence of SD-WAN-style connectivity with a full zero trust security stack delivered from the cloud.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing SASE with SD-WAN -- SD-WAN focuses on WAN connectivity optimization, while SASE bundles in the full security stack (firewall, SWG, ZTNA).
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: REST: lightweight, simple, fast, commonly preferred for general use. SOAP: XML-based, built-in error handling and transaction support, preferred in financial/government/telecom for data integrity.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Choosing the wrong API style for a compliance-heavy environment could sacrifice the transactional integrity SOAP is designed to provide.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming REST is always the better choice because it's more common -- SOAP's built-in transactional integrity and error handling make it preferred in regulated industries.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Authentication -> Authorization -> Input Validation -> Security Measures.
flashcards.why_it_matters: This sequence ensures identity and permission are established before any data processing or attack-prevention checks occur.
flashcards.common_trap: Running input validation or security checks before confirming the requestor's identity and permissions -- the order matters for both security and efficiency.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.term: Asset Identification vs. Management vs. Attestation
flashcards.definition: Identification: cataloging assets (Nmap/Nessus). Management: ongoing monitoring/maintenance (WSUS/Ansible/Intune). Attestation: verifying security posture/compliance (EDR/SIEM/Tenable).
flashcards.why_it_matters: These three asset-control activities map to different tool categories and different points in the zero trust asset lifecycle.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating asset identification and asset attestation as the same activity -- identification catalogs what exists, attestation verifies its compliance posture.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.term: Preventative vs. Detective vs. Proactive Cloud Controls
flashcards.definition: Preventative (IAM, MFA) stop incidents before they occur. Detective (logging/monitoring) detect breaches as/after they happen. Proactive (assessments, scans, threat intel) anticipate and address threats before they appear.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Recognizing which category a specific tool falls into helps map cloud security architecture questions to the right control type.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing proactive controls (anticipating future threats via assessments) with preventative controls (actively stopping an incident in real time, like MFA blocking an unauthorized login).
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.term: Forward Proxy vs. Reverse Proxy CASB
flashcards.definition: Forward proxy CASB sits at the edge of the user's network; reverse proxy CASB sits between the user and the cloud service and requires the cloud service to support that configuration.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The deployment mode affects which cloud services can be protected and how transparent the CASB is to end users.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any CASB deployment mode works with any cloud service -- reverse proxy CASB specifically requires cloud-service-side support.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Ansible: YAML playbooks, agentless, focused on configuration management/app deployment. Terraform: Infrastructure as Code tool for provisioning cloud infrastructure declaratively.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are common DevSecOps tools but solve different problems -- provisioning infrastructure (Terraform) vs. configuring it (Ansible).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Ansible requires agent software on managed servers -- it explicitly uses an agentless architecture.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.term: Serverless: Workloads vs. Functions vs. Resources
flashcards.definition: Workloads: the tasks/operations executed. Functions: individual, lightweight, stateless units of work (often microservices). Resources: underlying compute/storage/network the provider manages.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishing these three layers clarifies where security responsibility and configuration effort apply in a serverless architecture.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating 'function' and 'workload' as synonyms -- a workload can be composed of multiple functions executed as needed.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Batch processing collects data over a fixed period (e.g., eight hours) and processes it in bulk. Stream processing collects and analyzes data in near real-time, reducing analysis delay.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The choice directly impacts how quickly a security team can detect and respond to threats in specialized-system environments.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming batch processing is obsolete and never used -- it remains relevant in some legacy specialized-system environments despite stream processing's real-time advantage.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: Interception-based, memory-based, and log-based -- performing network sniffing, memory scraping, reading system tables, and analyzing database logs.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Knowing these three methods helps identify what technique a given DAM tool implementation is using to detect unauthorized database access.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing DAM's three methods with generic IDS detection categories (signature/anomaly-based) -- DAM's methods are specifically interception/memory/log-based.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: A Distributed Control System (DCS) interconnects multiple ICS for efficient large-scale control (manufacturing, utilities, military). SCADA is a subset of ICS for remote monitoring/control across wide geographic areas (energy, water, telecom) using cellular/satellite/VPN.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both extend ICS capability but at different scopes -- DCS for interconnected local/large-scale control, SCADA for wide-area remote monitoring.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating DCS and SCADA as synonyms -- DCS is about interconnecting ICS units, while SCADA is specifically about wide-area remote monitoring and control.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.term: Unsupported vs. Obsolete vs. Unable-to-Secure vs. Highly Constrained Systems
flashcards.definition: Unsupported: no vendor updates/patches. Obsolete: outdated, incompatible architecture. Unable to secure: design limitations prevent modern protections. Highly constrained: limited processing/memory/connectivity.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Each category calls for a different compensating control strategy, so misclassifying a legacy system can lead to the wrong mitigation approach.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating all four legacy-system categories as interchangeable -- each describes a distinct root cause requiring a different security approach.
flashcards.source: SecurityX CAS-005 training notes

flashcards.definition: In Common Criteria evaluations, a Protection Profile describes the threats a product category must defend against and the required countermeasures; a Security Target describes how a specific vendor's product actually meets those requirements.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam frequently tests whether you can distinguish 'what must be defended against' (Protection Profile) from 'how this specific product does it' (Security Target) versus the EAL, which only measures evaluation rigor.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing EAL (depth of evaluation) with Protection Profile/Security Target (content of the evaluation) -- a high EAL does not by itself tell you what threats were assessed.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Security in Systems

flashcards.definition: A structured inventory of every component, library, and dependency in a software application, each identified by name, version, and a unique identifier (e.g., a hash), including transitive dependencies.
flashcards.why_it_matters: SBoMs let organizations detect hidden, outdated, or tampered components across the full dependency graph -- not just direct dependencies.
flashcards.common_trap: Thinking an SBoM only lists direct dependencies -- it also tracks transitive dependencies (what your dependencies themselves depend on).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Security in Systems

flashcards.definition: SAST analyzes static source code/binaries without execution; DAST tests a running application by simulating attacks; IAST is a hybrid that monitors the app during active use for real-time feedback.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam tests matching each method to its testing phase (pre-deployment: SAST, DAST, IAST) and its execution state (static vs. running vs. actively exercised).
flashcards.common_trap: Mixing up IAST (requires active exercising, hybrid) with RASP (post-deployment, production runtime protection) -- IAST is still a pre-deployment testing method.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Security in Systems

flashcards.definition: A post-deployment security technology that operates from within a running application in production to detect and stop attacks in real time, even those bypassing external defenses.
flashcards.why_it_matters: RASP is the only listed technique that provides live, in-application protection after deployment, but it comes with a real performance cost.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming RASP replaces pre-deployment testing (SAST/DAST/IAST) -- it is a complementary, production-only control, not a substitute for earlier testing.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Security in Systems

flashcards.definition: Canary testing exposes a change to a limited audience in production to observe real-world behavior before full rollout; regression testing re-runs existing tests after a merge to confirm nothing broke.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are CI/CD testing concepts, but canary is about controlled production exposure while regression is about protecting existing functionality after a code change.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating 'phased rollout to a subset of users' (canary) and 'confirm old features still work' (regression) as the same concept -- they solve different problems.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Security in Systems

flashcards.definition: A U.S. Department of Defense initiative certifying that specific manufacturing facilities meet strict security standards (access control, supply chain security, audits) to produce hardware components vital to national security.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Only Trusted Foundry-certified facilities may legally produce certain DoD-critical hardware components -- a key hardware supply chain assurance control.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing this with Common Criteria certification (which evaluates a product's security capability, not the manufacturing facility's trustworthiness).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Security in Systems

flashcards.definition: A documented three-pass data-wipe process used to ensure that data on storage media is completely overwritten and unrecoverable at end-of-life.
flashcards.why_it_matters: It's a specific, named secure-deletion standard distinct from generic 'NIST-compliant erasure' or cryptographic erasure -- exam questions may ask you to identify the exact 'three-pass' method by name.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing this with cryptographic erasure, which destroys the encryption key rather than overwriting data multiple times.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 7: Security in Systems

flashcards.term: TPM vs. HSM vs. Secure Enclave
flashcards.definition: TPM: motherboard chip securing a single physical machine's boot/keys. HSM: dedicated appliance/card managing crypto operations across many machines enterprise-wide. Secure Enclave: Apple-specific isolated processor for keys/biometrics/transactions.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam tests picking the right root-of-trust technology for scope: single device (TPM), enterprise-wide (HSM), or Apple-specific isolated environment (Secure Enclave).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming an HSM and TPM are interchangeable -- HSMs are expensive, standalone, and multi-machine; TPMs are per-device motherboard chips.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 10: Hardware Security

flashcards.definition: Secure Boot actively verifies digital signatures and blocks components that fail verification (Windows-only). Measured Boot records hashes of boot components into the TPM as a verifiable log but does not block anything itself.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A classic exam distinction: Secure Boot 'blocks,' Measured Boot 'records/logs' for later attestation.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming Measured Boot halts the boot process on detecting tampering -- it does not; it only logs that something changed.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 10: Hardware Security

flashcards.definition: Intel Trusted Execution Technology validates that the software environment is secure before sensitive applications run. AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization encrypts data inside VMs so a compromised hypervisor can't expose guest contents.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are CPU security extensions but protect against different threats: TXT validates the pre-execution environment; SEV protects VM memory confidentiality from the hypervisor itself.
flashcards.common_trap: Mixing up which vendor's extension protects against a compromised hypervisor (AMD SEV) versus which validates environment integrity before execution (Intel TXT).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 10: Hardware Security

flashcards.definition: Windows uses BitLocker (AES, relies on TPM); Linux uses LUKS via Cryptsetup (AES); macOS uses FileVault (OS-integrated full disk encryption).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Direct OS-to-tool recall questions are common; know all three by name and their key trait (BitLocker's TPM dependency, in particular).
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting that BitLocker specifically relies on the TPM, unlike LUKS/FileVault which don't have that same dependency called out.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 10: Hardware Security

flashcards.definition: SELinux enforces MAC via security contexts tagging User, Role, Type, and Level; setsebool toggles booleans, semanage manages policy for new app access, and audit2allow generates custom rules from logged denials.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam questions often ask which SELinux tool does what -- know that audit2allow specifically works FROM logged denials to build new rules.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing audit2allow (builds rules from denial logs) with semanage (manages existing policy for app access) or setsebool (toggles simple on/off settings).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 11: Endpoint and Server Security

flashcards.definition: EDR provides real-time, endpoint-level visibility, ML-based anomaly detection, and automated isolation of a single compromised device. SIEM aggregates and correlates logs across many devices/sources for centralized detection, audits, and forensics.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A frequently tested distinction: EDR acts at the endpoint (detect + isolate that device); SIEM acts at the enterprise log level (aggregate + correlate across everything).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming SIEM can automatically isolate a compromised endpoint the way EDR does -- SIEM's core functions are aggregation and correlation, not automated endpoint remediation.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 11: Endpoint and Server Security

flashcards.definition: MDM (Mobile Device Management) is the specific technical toolset enforcing compliance on mobile devices (app control, password mgmt, MFA, token-based access, patch mgmt, remote wipe, geofencing). EMM (Enterprise Mobility Management) is the broader strategic umbrella of policies/procedures.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam may test whether you recognize MDM as the 'how' (technology) nested inside EMM's 'what/why' (strategy).
flashcards.common_trap: Treating MDM and EMM as fully interchangeable terms -- MDM is a subset/technology layer within the broader EMM strategy.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 11: Endpoint and Server Security

flashcards.definition: Attack Surface Monitoring continuously observes entry points/devices/services (Nmap, Nessus, Qualys, SIEM, EDR tools) to detect gaps as they appear. Attack Surface Reduction actively removes unnecessary services, closes ports, and hardens systems (CIS Benchmarks, GPOs, Chef, SCCM/WSUS).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Monitoring = passive/ongoing detection; Reduction = active minimization -- know which named tools belong to each (Nmap/Nessus/Qualys/SIEM/EDR = monitoring; CIS Benchmarks/GPO/Chef/SCCM/WSUS/Spacewalk = reduction).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming monitoring tools like Nmap/Nessus perform the actual hardening -- they detect gaps; CIS Benchmarks and configuration management tools perform the reduction/hardening itself.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 11: Endpoint and Server Security

flashcards.definition: A Microsoft tool that automatically generates complex, unique local administrator passwords per Windows endpoint and stores them securely in Active Directory.
flashcards.why_it_matters: LAPS is the specific Windows-side answer whenever a question describes automated, unique, AD-stored local admin password rotation across many endpoints.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing LAPS (Windows local admin passwords) with sudo/etc/sudoers (Linux privilege elevation) -- they solve the same category of problem (privilege management) on different OSes with different mechanisms.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 11: Endpoint and Server Security

flashcards.definition: MD5 (128-bit, broken/insecure) -> SHA-2 (SHA-1/224/256/384/512) -> SHA-3 (latest, up to 120 rounds); RIPEMD (128/160/256/320-bit, non-government origin, used in PGP/Bitcoin).
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam tests recognizing which hash family fits a scenario -- especially RIPEMD's non-government/privacy-advocate angle and MD5's known collision weakness.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming SHA-2 and SHA-3 are interchangeable or that MD5 is still acceptable for security purposes -- MD5 is explicitly no longer considered secure.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 12: Data Security Concepts

flashcards.term: Tokenization vs. Data Masking vs. Cryptographic Erase
flashcards.definition: Tokenization: reversible, replaces data with tokens mapped elsewhere. Data Masking: not reversible, replaces data with generic placeholders. Cryptographic Erase: destroys encryption keys to make data unrecoverable.
flashcards.why_it_matters: These three data protection techniques look similar but have very different reversibility properties -- a frequent exam discriminator.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming data masking is reversible like tokenization -- it explicitly is not; only tokenization preserves a reference back to the original data.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 12: Data Security Concepts

flashcards.definition: From coarsest to finest: disk-level (BitLocker/FileVault) -> block-level (SANs/virtual partitions) -> file-level (individual files) -> record-level (individual database records, most granular).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Knowing the granularity order helps match the right encryption type to a scenario's specific protection need (e.g., per-record protection in a high-security database = record-level).
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing block-level (fixed-size storage units, common in SANs) with disk-level (whole disk/partition) -- they sound similar but operate at different layers.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 12: Data Security Concepts

flashcards.term: IPsec: AH vs. ESP, Transport vs. Tunnel
flashcards.definition: AH provides authentication/integrity only (no encryption); ESP adds encryption for confidentiality. Transport Mode encrypts only the payload; Tunnel Mode encrypts both payload and headers.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A classic exam matrix: pick the AH/ESP and Transport/Tunnel combination that satisfies a stated requirement (e.g., 'encrypt headers too' = Tunnel Mode).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming AH provides encryption -- it only provides authentication and integrity, not confidentiality; that's ESP's role.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 12: Data Security Concepts

flashcards.definition: GDPR requires organizations to report data breaches to authorities within 72 hours, and mandates data protection by design and by default plus data minimization and explicit consent.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The specific '72 hours' figure is a commonly tested factual detail distinguishing GDPR from other privacy frameworks like CCPA.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing GDPR's 72-hour breach window with CCPA's separate requirements (clear privacy notices, honoring user data requests) -- CCPA does not specify this same breach window in these notes.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 12: Data Security Concepts

flashcards.definition: AES (current standard, 128/192/256-bit, hardware-accelerated) > 3DES (112-bit effective, banking legacy) > DES (56-bit, broken) > Blowfish (32-448-bit, superseded by Twofish) > RC4 (stream, broken, SSL/WEP legacy) > ChaCha20 (modern RC4 replacement).
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam often gives a scenario and expects you to name the specific legacy or modern algorithm being described, including resource tradeoffs (e.g., 3DES is resource-heavy; ChaCha20 balances security and low resource use).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any algorithm named 'DES-something' is automatically insecure -- 3DES, while dated and resource-heavy, is a real improvement over plain DES (112-bit effective key), even though AES has replaced it.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 13: Cryptographic Types

flashcards.definition: A symmetric technique offering theoretically perfect secrecy using a truly random key exactly as long as the message, used only once; its core challenge is securely distributing that key.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam questions may ask which method offers 'unbreakable'/'perfect secrecy' encryption -- the OTP is the specific answer, with key reuse and distribution as its Achilles' heel.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any strong modern cipher (like AES-256) offers the same theoretical guarantee as a one-time pad -- only a correctly used OTP offers true perfect secrecy.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 13: Cryptographic Types

flashcards.definition: RSA: factoring problem, 1024-4096-bit keys, SSL/TLS/signatures. Diffie-Hellman: key exchange only, no built-in authentication, vulnerable to logjam/MITM. ECC: Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem, RSA-equivalent security with far smaller keys (256-bit ECC ~ 3072-bit RSA).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Each algorithm has a distinct underlying hard math problem and a distinct primary use case -- expect exam questions that test matching algorithm to math problem to use case.
flashcards.common_trap: Forgetting that Diffie-Hellman provides no authentication on its own -- it must be paired with digital certificates to prevent MITM attacks.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 13: Cryptographic Types

flashcards.definition: ECDSA uses elliptic curves for digital signing/verification (authenticity). ECDH uses elliptic curves for secure key exchange (confidentiality setup), letting two parties derive a shared secret over an insecure channel.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both are elliptic-curve variants but serve different cryptographic goals -- signing/authenticity (ECDSA) versus key exchange (ECDH) -- a common exam discriminator.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating ECDSA and ECDH as interchangeable just because both start with 'EC' -- their purposes (signing vs. key exchange) are distinct.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 13: Cryptographic Types

flashcards.definition: Digital signatures (private key signs, public key verifies) provide authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation -- but NOT confidentiality; the message must separately be encrypted with the receiver's public key for confidentiality.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A very frequently tested point: signing a message does not automatically make it confidential.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming a digitally signed email is automatically encrypted/confidential -- signing and encrypting are separate steps requiring separate keys (signer's private key vs. receiver's public key).
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 13: Cryptographic Types

flashcards.definition: Combines Ownership Factors (something you have: smartphone, smart card, hardware token) with Biometric Factors (something you are: fingerprint, face) using public key cryptography, eliminating knowledge-based secrets.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Passwordless authentication's main risk is biometric impersonation, mitigated by low false-positive rates and well-tested technology, plus layering with MFA.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming passwordless authentication removes the need for MFA entirely -- MFA is still recommended to further enhance security in passwordless schemes.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 13: Cryptographic Types

flashcards.definition: DV (Domain Validation): basic encryption, verifies domain ownership only. OV (Organization Validation): adds organizational legitimacy checks. EV (Extended Validation): most rigorous validation process, highest assurance.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios often describe a validation requirement's rigor level and expect you to name DV/OV/EV correctly.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming DV certificates verify organizational legitimacy -- DV only confirms domain ownership and provides basic encryption, nothing more.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 14: PKI Architecture

flashcards.definition: A Critical extension must be understood/enforced by any application using the certificate (or the cert is rejected); a Non-Critical extension may be safely ignored if unrecognized.
flashcards.why_it_matters: This is a core X.509 concept the exam tests directly -- know which marking forces enforcement versus which allows graceful ignoring.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming 'critical' means 'important' in a general sense rather than its precise technical meaning: mandatory understanding/enforcement by the relying application.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 14: PKI Architecture

flashcards.definition: .pem: common text format for individual certs/keys (often DER-encoded). .p12/PKCS#12: bundles certs+private key, encrypted, cross-platform. .pfx: like .p12 but Microsoft-associated. .p7b: certificate chain ONLY, no private keys.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Distinguishing which format can/cannot carry a private key (.p7b cannot) is a frequently tested detail.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing .p12/.pfx (both bundle certs AND private keys) with .p7b (certificate chain only, no private key) -- a key discriminator for secure distribution scenarios.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 14: PKI Architecture

flashcards.term: OCSP vs. OCSP Stapling vs. CRL
flashcards.definition: OCSP: client queries a responder in real time for one certificate's revocation status. OCSP Stapling: the server itself provides a signed, cached proof of validity to the client (faster, more private). CRL: a CA-maintained list of all revoked certificate serial numbers.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Know the performance/privacy tradeoffs: OCSP Stapling avoids the client contacting a third party for every connection, unlike plain OCSP.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming CRLs and OCSP are the same mechanism -- CRL is a downloadable list checked against, while OCSP is a real-time per-certificate query protocol.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 14: PKI Architecture

flashcards.definition: Certificate Pinning embeds a known-good certificate/public key in an application to defend against on-path attacks, bypassing the normal CA chain of trust. HPKP was a deprecated browser-level implementation of this idea.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Know that HPKP is deprecated specifically because misconfiguration could cause service disruptions -- a commonly tested 'why was this retired' fact.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming certificate pinning still relies on the standard CA hierarchy -- its whole point is to bypass that hierarchy for a specific, hardcoded trust anchor.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 14: PKI Architecture

flashcards.definition: Key Stretching (PBKDF2, Bcrypt) strengthens ONE weak key/password via iterative salted hashing to resist brute-force. Key Splitting divides ONE key into MULTIPLE parts held by different parties/systems to reduce compromise risk.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Both defend keys but through opposite mechanisms -- strengthening a single key's resistance to attack vs. distributing trust across multiple key fragments.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing 'stretching' (repeated processing of one key) with 'splitting' (dividing one key into separate pieces) -- they sound similar but solve different problems.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 15: Advanced Cryptographic Concepts

flashcards.definition: AEAD (e.g., AES-GCM) provides confidentiality+integrity+authenticity for a message plus associated data in a single operation. Envelope Encryption is a key-management pattern: a data key encrypts data, and a master key encrypts the data key.
flashcards.why_it_matters: AEAD is about WHAT properties one encryption operation guarantees; envelope encryption is about HOW keys are architected/managed across layers -- don't conflate the two.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming envelope encryption itself provides authenticity/integrity guarantees like AEAD does -- envelope encryption is purely a key-management layering strategy.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 15: Advanced Cryptographic Concepts

flashcards.definition: A property ensuring that compromising one session's (ephemeral) key does not compromise past or future sessions, since session keys are not derived from the server's long-term private key; commonly enabled via Diffie-Hellman, used in VPNs, TLS 1.3, SSH, and WPA3 (SAE).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Forward secrecy is a heavily tested exam concept -- know that it protects OTHER sessions, not the compromised session itself, and that DH-based ephemeral key exchange is the enabling mechanism.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming forward secrecy protects the compromised session itself from disclosure -- it does not; it only protects the confidentiality of OTHER (past/future) sessions.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 15: Advanced Cryptographic Concepts

flashcards.definition: Partially Homomorphic: specific operations only (e.g., addition OR multiplication). Somewhat Homomorphic: a limited set of operations, limited number of times. Fully Homomorphic: any computation, unlimited, but currently very slow.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios describing 'unlimited/any computation' point to Fully Homomorphic; 'just addition' points to Partially Homomorphic -- know the tier names and constraints.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any homomorphic encryption allows unlimited arbitrary computation -- only the Fully Homomorphic tier does, and it comes with a significant performance cost.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 15: Advanced Cryptographic Concepts

flashcards.definition: Lattice-based (LWE/Ring-LWE, multi-dimensional grids), Hash-based (hard-to-reverse hash functions), Multivariate Polynomial (nonlinear equation systems), Code-based (decoding random linear codes, good for large-scale systems), plus Quantum Key Distribution and Supersingular Isogeny Key Exchange -- all designed to resist quantum attacks that threaten DH and ECC.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam may ask which PQC family matches a described mathematical hard problem -- know the distinguishing basis of each family.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming PQC is a single algorithm rather than a family of distinct mathematical approaches, each with its own strengths, weaknesses, and practical maturity level.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 15: Advanced Cryptographic Concepts

flashcards.definition: Privileged Identity Management (PIM) focuses on granting elevated permissions only when necessary (just-in-time access). Privileged Access Management (PAM) controls/monitors that access with capabilities like automatic password rotation, session management, MFA enforcement, and auditing.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam may test the subtle distinction between PIM (identity/permission granting model) and PAM (the broader operational control/monitoring toolset), which the sudoers file relies on.
flashcards.common_trap: Treating PIM and PAM as fully identical concepts -- they overlap in purpose (least privilege, just-in-time access) but PAM includes broader operational controls like session monitoring and password rotation.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 16: Troubleshooting IAM

flashcards.definition: SAML: XML-based, exchanges auth/authz assertions between IdP and SP for SSO. OAuth: authorization framework issuing tokens so third parties access data without credentials. OpenID: authentication protocol letting users log into multiple services via one IdP.
flashcards.why_it_matters: These three federated identity technologies are frequently confused -- know that OAuth is about AUTHORIZATION (delegated access), while SAML and OpenID are about AUTHENTICATION/SSO.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming OAuth authenticates a user's identity the way OpenID or SAML does -- OAuth's core purpose is authorizing delegated access to resources, not asserting identity.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 16: Troubleshooting IAM

flashcards.definition: EAP-TLS (certificates both ends, no passwords, recommended) > PEAP / EAP-TTLS (server certificate creates encrypted tunnel, then CHAPv2/OTP or passwords inside) > EAP-FAST (Protected Access Credential instead of certificate, least secure of these) > legacy PAP (plaintext) and CHAP (challenge-response, no certs).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios describing 'certificates on both ends, no passwords' point to EAP-TLS; 'faster setup, no certificate needed' points to EAP-FAST (less secure).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming EAP-FAST's speed/ease of setup makes it equally secure to EAP-TLS -- it is explicitly considered less secure because it substitutes a Protected Access Credential for a certificate.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 16: Troubleshooting IAM

flashcards.definition: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) replaces WPA/WPA2's four-way handshake in WPA3, relies on forward secrecy, and uses the Dragonfly Algorithm (elliptic curve cryptography) to generate a shared secret and session key.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A commonly tested WPA3 fact: know that SAE specifically replaces the four-way handshake and inherently provides forward secrecy.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing SAE (WPA3's key exchange) with 802.1X/EAP (the broader enterprise network access authentication framework) -- SAE is specific to WPA3 personal/pre-shared-key-style authentication.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 16: Troubleshooting IAM

flashcards.definition: Switching Errors (Layer 2): Broadcast Storms (loops/STP misconfig), VLAN Mismatch (differing trunk VLANs), Duplex Mismatch (differing link duplex settings). Routing Errors (Layer 3): Routing Loops, Incorrect Subnet Masks, Route Flapping.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam tests whether you can correctly place a symptom at Layer 2 (switching) or Layer 3 (routing) -- a foundational network troubleshooting skill.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing a Broadcast Storm (Layer 2 loop issue, fixed via STP) with a Routing Loop (Layer 3 issue, a packet cycling between routers) -- they sound similar but are different layers and different fixes.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 17: Troubleshooting Network Infrastructure

flashcards.definition: IDS can sit on a mirrored port (out-of-line, observes copied traffic). IPS must be placed directly inline with traffic it needs to actively block, especially in high-traffic/sensitive areas.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Placement is explicitly called out as a common source of IDS/IPS failure -- an IPS placed out-of-band cannot actually block anything.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming IDS and IPS have the same placement requirements -- only the IPS strictly requires inline placement since only it actively intervenes.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 17: Troubleshooting Network Infrastructure

flashcards.definition: SPF: authorizes which mail servers can send for a domain. DKIM: adds a digital signature verifying message integrity/sender authenticity. DMARC: enforces policy (reject/quarantine/flag) based on SPF+DKIM results and provides reporting.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A very commonly tested trio -- know that DMARC sits ON TOP of SPF and DKIM results rather than being an independent, competing mechanism.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming any one of SPF, DKIM, or DMARC alone fully prevents email spoofing -- they're complementary layers, with DMARC specifically depending on the other two's results.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 17: Troubleshooting Network Infrastructure

flashcards.term: DNSSEC vs. Sinkholing vs. Zone Transfer Security (TSIG)
flashcards.definition: DNSSEC: digitally signs DNS data (private key signs, public key verifies) to prevent cache poisoning. TSIG: authenticates zone transfers between authorized DNS servers. Sinkholing: redirects malicious traffic to a controlled server.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Three distinct DNS security mechanisms addressing different threats -- data integrity (DNSSEC), replication security (TSIG), and active malicious-traffic redirection (sinkholing).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming DNSSEC secures zone transfers -- that is TSIG's specific role; DNSSEC authenticates the DNS data/responses themselves.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 17: Troubleshooting Network Infrastructure

flashcards.term: Gateway Types: XML, API, NAT, VPN
flashcards.definition: XML Gateway: app-layer firewall inspecting XML messages (inbound pattern detection, outbound data leak prevention). API Gateway: centralizes/manages API functions in the cloud. NAT Gateway: gives private VPC subnets outbound-only internet access. VPN Gateway: bridges remote sites/networks/devices in a VPN.
flashcards.why_it_matters: A frequently missed exam topic (per Josh's own missed-question history) -- expect a scenario naming a specific gateway function and requiring you to pick the matching gateway type.
flashcards.common_trap: Confusing a NAT Gateway (outbound internet access for private subnets) with a VPN Gateway (bridges two or more networks/sites together) -- they solve very different connectivity problems.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Missed Practice-Exam Question Explanations

flashcards.definition: Application (requests/network info) -> Control (routing, prioritization, security, forwarding decisions) -> Infrastructure (physical devices executing instructions) -> Management (monitoring/oversight for admins).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Another historically missed exam topic -- know each layer's specific responsibility, especially that the Control layer is where routing/security decisions are actually made.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming the Infrastructure layer makes routing decisions -- it only executes what the Control layer decides; the physical devices don't decide the routing/security policy themselves.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Missed Practice-Exam Question Explanations

flashcards.definition: Bash: variables, strings, arrays (zero-indexed). PowerShell: variables, arrays, hash tables, objects. Python: lists (ordered, mutable), tuples (ordered, immutable), dictionaries (key-value), sets (unique, unordered).
flashcards.why_it_matters: Exam questions often describe a specific data-handling need and ask which language/structure fits -- know each language's distinctive structures (e.g., Python's immutable tuple, Bash's zero-indexed array).
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming all languages index arrays the same way -- Bash explicitly uses zero-based indexing, which is called out as a specific, testable detail.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 20: Automated Security Operations

flashcards.definition: A simplified, syntax-free, high-level outline of a script's logic and steps, used during the design phase before actual code is written in any specific language.
flashcards.why_it_matters: Recognizing pseudocode's role (planning before syntax) versus an actual script helps answer 'what should be done first' sequencing questions.
flashcards.common_trap: Assuming pseudocode must follow the syntax rules of a specific language -- its entire purpose is to be language-agnostic.
flashcards.source: Dion Training SecurityX (CAS-005) Course Notes, Section 20: Automated Security Operations

flashcards.term: Config File Formats: YAML, XML, JSON, TOML
flashcards.definition: YAML: readable, hierarchical, common in cloud deployments. XML: highly structured, tag-based, strict hierarchy (web service security policies). JSON: lightweight, key-value, popular for API data interchange. TOML: simple, readable, ini-like, best for smaller tools.
flashcards.why_it_matters: The exam may describe a use case (API config, web service policy, cloud deployment, small tool) and expect you to name the matching format.
